#2653. Darius Acuff Jr. isn't a perfect rookie, but he may be just what the Kings need right now

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The usage rate leaders list through the first two and a half weeks of the NBA season features some familiar and expected names: Luka Dončić, Anthony Edwards (four games), Victor Wembanyama, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Stephen Curry round out the top five, with Brandon Miller and Jayson Tatum not far behind.

However, the name below them might come as a surprise. Kings rookie guard Darius Acuff Jr., who has a 31.6% usage rate through the first eight games, is No. 8 on the list.

The only other rookie in the top 40 is Bulls forward Caleb Wilson (No. 38).

Here are the last five players to win NBA Rookie of the Year, along with their respective usage rates.

Even with a sample size that represents barely 10% of the season, what Acuff is doing will likely be sustainable, as he's being asked to do more than any rookie in his class on the offensive end of the floor. It's for that reason that his play has drawn eyeballs and why everybody seems to have an opinion — whether it's positive, negative, or maybe even somewhere in between — on him.

Is the 19-year-old guard a perfect rookie? Absolutely not. But he is just eight games into his NBA career and is posting numbers that get him in the same conversation as players like Dončić, LeBron James and Oscar Robertson.

After finishing with 22 points and 12 assists in a loss to the Lakers on Wednesday, Acuff became the fastest NBA player in NBA history to reach at least 200 points and 50 assists. It's hard to imagine he won't be writing his name into the record books across his rookie season.

As someone who watched Acuff throughout his entire college career at Arkansas, I'm not surprised to see the numbers he is putting up in the NBA. Acuff was just the second SEC player (and the first since Pete Maravich) to average at least 22 points and six assists per game in a season.

John Calipari has coached plenty of outstanding one-and-done guards during his time at Memphis, Kentucky and Arkansas, including Gilgeous-Alexander, Devin Booker, Derrick Rose, De'Aaron Fox, Jamal Murray, John Wall, and Tyrese Maxey. Simply put: if you're an elite high school guard prospect, you want to play for Coach Cal.

Acuff's season at Arkansas had him in the conversation for the best freshman guard Calipari has coached. Does that mean he's going to become a two-time NBA MVP like SGA or a multi-time NBA All-Star like the other names on that list? The jury is still out, but his college production — on both ends of the floor — is similar to what we are seeing play out in the NBA.

For starters, Arkansas didn't have a deep roster, which meant Acuff was on the floor a lot. He played just over 35 minutes per game, which is slightly less than he's playing with Sacramento right now. The same depth issues Acuff experienced at Arkansas are what he's dealing with in the NBA with his new team.

The Kings don't have a true backup point guard, which means Acuff is playing more than anybody else on the roster. When Acuff comes off the floor, Sacramento has been playing Malik Monk as the de facto point guard — a role he has filled in spot minutes throughout his time with the Kings.

Ben Simmons was also expected to be in Sacramento's starting lineup this season, where he could've taken on some of the ball-handling duties in the first and second units, but he suffered a torn Achilles days before the 2026-27 season began. That leaves Acuff, most nights, to play the entire fourth quarter and run the offense with a team full of players who can't create their own shot.

While Acuff's offensive game is as good as anybody in his class, the knock on him during the pre-draft process was his defense. It showed up throughout his time at Arkansas, but in Acuff's defense (no pun intended), he was asked to be the primary engine of the offense while staying on the floor for most of the game.

In Sacramento, it's been more of the same.

Acuff isn't a strong defender, and projecting him as a net-neutral defender over the course of his career would be a big win for his development. The offensive end is where Acuff is going to make his money. His processing skills for his age are elite and will only get better.

Acuff to Sacramento was one of the worst-kept secrets throughout the entire pre-draft cycle. The connections between his family and Kings general manager Scott Perry run deep: Perry coached Darius Acuff Sr. when he played at Eastern Kentucky in the 1990s.

After Sacramento fell in the draft lottery and landed pick No. 7, it became almost too obvious that Acuff would end up a King. The Clippers coveted Keaton Wagler early in the cycle, while Brooklyn liked the shooting upside of Mikel Brown Jr. Even though the Kings were said to be deciding between Acuff and Kingston Flemings, the former felt inevitable if Acuff was indeed available when Sacramento was on the board.

With that context, it's easy to understand why he is being handed the keys to the offense immediately, despite being on a roster that includes former NBA All-Stars Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis. LaVine has the second-highest usage rate on the team (25.6%), while Sabonis — who thrived as the hub of Sacramento's offense during the 2022-23 season— has a usage rate of just 15.7%.

Even with a roster that might not look 1-7 bad on paper, the Kings simply don't have enough shot creation and shot-making outside of Acuff and LaVine. The stat that stands out? Only 23 of Acuff's 189 shots have been catch-and-shoot attempts, per Synergy. At Arkansas, Acuff thrived in the catch-and-shoot department, shooting 50% (60 of 120) in that category.

Please don’t try to hate on Acuff’s shot attempts if you don’t watch the Kings 😭Directing traffic for his own teammates, & they end up needing him to create a quality shot. He’s literally his entire team’s system. James Harden type shit. pic.twitter.com/ag5MWTcWAE

Acuff is averaging 23.6 shot attempts per game, which ranks second in the NBA, behind only Gilgeous-Alexander. While that stat might pop, most of the looks Acuff is getting have been a massive improvement from his NBA debut, where he shot 5 of 24 against the Clippers.

For a smaller guard, Acuff has done a great job of getting to the paint; he's shooting 25 of 52 (48.1%) at the rim. Acuff is also getting a healthy number of 3-point attempts. He shot 44% from beyond the arc at Arkansas, but has connected on just 30.8% of his 3-point attempts so far. Rookie guards are historically inefficient, so it shouldn't be that much of a cause for concern.

Sacramento seems to be waiting on the 2027 offseason to take a step toward a proper rebuild, though the front office has reportedly been trying to move LaVine and Sabonis — the two highest-paid players on the team — since Perry took over as GM in 2024. LaVine and De'Andre come off the books this summer, while Sabonis and Malik Monk (player option) are free agents in 2028.

The blueprint for building a team around Acuff — a player who can score at will and be the offensive engine for a team — should be what the Knicks have done with Jalen Brunson. New York surrounded Brunson with 3-and-D wings, which takes the pressure off him on the defensive end of the floor. Sacramento has just one true 3-and-D wing on the roster: Keegan Murray, who is currently out with an ankle injury.

With several high-priced veterans on the roster, this will be Sacramento's short-term future. The No. 1 priority this season for Sacramento is developing Acuff so when the big names come off the books and the team has cap space, the franchise can properly build a team around him.

One popular comparison Acuff has drawn, dating back to the pre-draft cycle, is Cam Thomas. No disrespect at all to Thomas — who was one of the best pure shotmakers and scorers in the league when he played — but Acuff is by far a more advanced passer and facilitator for his age.

Acuff is averaging seven assists per game, which ranks 12th in the league. He is also averaging 12.4 potential assists per game, per the NBA's tracking data, which ranks 11th. Acuff at Arkansas was an elite facilitator despite being a high-volume scorer. Over the last few games, Acuff has been making an effort to get his teammates involved in the high pick-and-roll.

This clip from Wednesday's loss to the Lakers is exactly the kind of play Acuff is making that won't show up on the box score: he falls over while making a cross-court pass to a wide-open shooter (Monk) who missed a 3-pointer. Acuff finished with 12 assists against the Lakers, but had 17 potential assists, per the tracking data.

Darius Acuff ter 7 assistências nesse jogo é um crime federal.O garoto tá fazendo tudo pra achar visuais para os companheiros de time e nada cai.Olha isso irmão… revoltante uma parada dessas. pic.twitter.com/TIu2m3Gm1X

Let's go back to Thomas, who didn't have a game with more than four assists during his rookie season. Acuff has recorded at least five assists in six of his first eight games, including two with over 12 assists.

Acuff's passing was one of his strengths throughout his college career. He is a very good lob passer who routinely made tough cross-court or skip passes with multiple defenders in the area. While Acuff is known for scoring, his passing is underrated.

Acuff isn't a perfect rookie, but he isn't even 20 years old and Sacramento projects as one of the worst teams in the NBA. The Kings will happily trade the good for the bad if he continues to develop and post the numbers he's putting up.

#2652. Chargers' Mike McDaniel to begin calling play from the booth: Desperation move or possible fix?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

No team in the NFL has fallen flatter than the Los Angeles Chargers in 2026. Coming into the campaign, the offense was expected to be supercharged with the arrival of Mike McDaniel as the new offensive coordinator. The hope was that McDaniel would elevate Justin Herbert and the rest of the unit to new heights, but the polar opposite has happened. The offense ranks at the bottom of the league, the club is 0-7 entering Week 9 and the seat under McDaniel is piping hot.

All that has led to a shakeup in how McDaniel will call plays going forward. He told reporters on Thursday he plans to work from the coaching box as opposed to being on the sideline.

"One of the things I talked with [Jim Harbaugh] about, one of the things that I want to try is call plays from the box to kind of see adjustments for myself and communicate to the position coaches appropriately what we can focus on between series," said McDaniel. "I'm being very open-minded with all things. Not trying to prove or justify anything that ultimately leads to underwhelming results. You do your best. You make decisions from a point of information, expertise, and integrity, and then you understand that no one is going to care unless something changes.

"Seems like a good action to take based on how things have gone this year and realistically something that I've only brought up because of ... I'm very confident in the rest of the offensive coaching staff and how they're able to set the tone and communicate information on the sidelines. So I feel a little bit more comfortable to try that."

The Chargers host the Houston Texans at SoFi Stadium in Week 9.

This feels like a grasping-at-straws type of move for the Chargers and McDaniel. While seeing things from a different point of view in the coach's booth may bring a different perspective, it's hard to imagine it making a night-and-day difference. On top of their winless record, the offense has been abysmal, ranking last in the NFL in points per game and 28th in total yards per game. Moreover, the team is 30th in yards per play.

Coming into Week 9, Los Angeles has yet to score a touchdown in the past two games. The last time they found the end zone was back in Week 5 in the third quarter against the Broncos. Since then, they've gone 27 straight drives without a touchdown.

As for Justin Hebert, he's regressed dramatically under McDaniel. The Chargers quarterback has thrown five touchdowns and 10 interceptions through seven games. He's particularly struggled late in games, notching six turnovers and zero total touchdowns in the fourth quarter this season.

These feel like foundational and fundamental problems for the Chargers that a view from above in the booth won't fix, but it's a worthwhile — albeit a last-ditch — effort by McDaniel.

There's only so many other moves that the Chargers can make before ultimately pulling the plug on the McDaniel tenure. If the offense continues to look lackluster in the team's Week 9 matchup against the Texans despite this move to the booth, it wouldn't be surprising if that were the straw that broke the camel's back and led to McDaniel's firing.

This shakeup feels like an acknowledgment by the Chargers and McDaniel that the OC is on shaky ground. This is a move to see if anything changes and, if it doesn't, they make the decision that Jim Harbaugh has been reluctant to make up to this point.

After all, the Texans' defense hasn't been as lethal as it was a year ago, allowing three 30-point games so far this season after allowing just one in 2025. They also have allowed three 300-yard passers to this point in the season after allowing none last year.

If the Chargers make the Texans look more like the 2025 version of themselves, it'll only be further ammunition to move on from McDaniel, particularly as the Chargers will have extended time before they kick off Week 10 against the Baltimore Ravens next Monday night.

#2651. Biggest MLB offseason questions: How long will lockout last? Will we see a free agency frenzy?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Not so long ago, the Milwaukee Brewers were crowned World Series champions, and at the moment of the last out, the 2026-27 Major League offseason began. So let's talk about that.

The winter ahead is one shot through with uncertainty, as labor strife figures to roil the sport and perhaps even compromise the 2027 season. Those matters, vital as they are, won't be the only story, and we'll still have the familiar presences of free agency and trade talk to sustain us.

To set the scene for all that's ahead in advance of the 2027 campaign – good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – we're here to take a look at the five questions that will inform an offseason that's going to be quite unusual and – for good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – probably unforgettable. Let's explore those five queries right now …

The current collective bargaining agreement – or CBA, the accord that governs the working relationship between clubs/owners and players – is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year. At that time, MLB owners are all but certain to lock out the players. That's a labor stoppage, and that means the offseason will be brought to a sudden halt. The lockout, the purpose of which is to preempt a players' strike, will last until a new CBA is agreed to. Agreeing to a new CBA will be no simple matter, and owners and their hireling, commissioner Rob Manfred, are pushing for a cap on team payrolls. The players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, have never shown any willingness to agree to a cap-and-floor system. There are a lot of other issues to iron out, as the CBA is an all-encompassing document, but the fight over a cap will be what drags out the lockout.

The heart of the matter is whether the lockout will last long enough to push back, abbreviate, or – perish the thought – cancel entirely the 2027 season. The latter is the worst-case scenario and is highly unlikely, but it's a possibility, however remote. More of a threat is a 2027 season that doesn't span the usual 162 games.

We have a recent precedent to guide us. The last time the CBA was up for negotiation during the offseason of 2021-22, owners locked out the players for 99 days. That meant a shortened spring training by about two and a half weeks and forced the regular season calendar to be compressed, albeit while still preserving the 162-game docket. As such, we can say that if the lockout lasts beyond the middle of March 2027, then we'll likely lose regular-season games.

For further context, here's a brief history of modern labor stoppages in the sport:

Just two, the 1981 and 1994-95 player strikes, significantly compromised seasons. The 1994-95 stoppage cost us the 1994 World Series, and it took years for the sport to recover from the resulting fan disaffection.

As for the 2027 season, the worst-case scenario may not be the loss of the entire season but rather the loss of 60 games off the regular-season slate. Here's the explanation from our recent Lockout 101 piece:

"… [I]f the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives."

Obviously, the hope is that the lockout doesn't even affect the spring training calendar, let alone cost us a major chunk of the regular season.

As noted, the big fight is over whether or not MLB will have a cap-and-floor structure moving forward, as is the case in the NFL, NBA, and NHL. Owners have tied every single proposal wrinkle to date to the players' acceptance of a cap. However, it remains highly unlikely, at least until further notice, that the union would ever agree to such a thing.

The other major issue is a likely restructuring of the revenue-sharing system. Specifically, the next CBA is highly likely to revise the system so that local broadcast revenues are shared much more evenly. Fortunately, there's already some common ground on this issue, and a reordering of that system would directly address the revenue disparities within MLB that are such a reliable source of consternation – and misinformation – without the grievous labor war that a continued cap push would force upon us.

Otherwise, some other key wrinkles and changes may come out of the wash. That list potentially includes:

This doesn't get into evergreen matters like an increase in the minimum salary, draft bonus pools, the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, and so forth. There's a lot to sort out, to say the least. The expectation is that the next CBA is going to lead to sweeping changes to the sport starting in 2027 and, perhaps by design, growing over time. Even if there's no cap and floor, the economic structure of MLB is almost certain to look very different after this winter.

Overall, this is one of the weakest free agent classes in living memory, but there is elite superstar value to be found at the tip-top with back-to-back (for the moment) American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

Skubal, who turns 30 on Nov. 20, remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and he's going to be paid like it. The expectation is that he'll wind up signing the largest pitcher contract in MLB history and perhaps also fetch the highest-ever annual salary for a pitcher. It's not out of the question that Skubal's next contract could approach or even surpass $400 million in total value. At those rates, the incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers and the free-spending New York Mets are the consensus favorites. The Chicago Cubs are also reportedly heavily interested in Skubal, and surprise bidders are always possible. Other notable free agent names include Freddy Peralta, Michael King, Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trevor Rogers, Adrian Morejon, and Teruaki Sato. Our ranking of the top 50 2026-27 free agents has you covered.

The "when" of all this is more complicated thanks to the upcoming lockout detailed above. Will premium free agents and their representatives rush to find some stability in advance of the stoppage, during which no major-league transactions will be permitted, or will they decide that the long game will be better for their markets? It's possible that the biggest spenders on the team side will look to make moves early, as the barrel of the next CBA figures to be leveled directly at them and their abundant revenues. Or maybe the unknown will have a chilling effect on spending before we arrive at the lockout.

The past is not always prelude, but let's note that we saw a flurry of spending leading up to the lockout of 2021-22. Indeed, in November 2021, MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents prior to the lockout. The Texas Rangers alone guaranteed $500 million to a new middle infield – Corey Seager and Marcus Semien – before the lockout put an end to such things. In all, teams put ink to paper on five nine-figure contracts prior to the 2021-22 lockout.

The comparisons may not entirely hold since this upcoming CBA should bring about a much more drastic re-ordering of the sport than the current expiring CBA did. As such, teams may proceed cautiously given all the uncertainties. Or, as just mentioned, they may seek to get business done before the ways of doing business change entirely. We'll see soon enough. If we do see the dollars start flying before the lockout, then the upcoming Nov. 10-12 general managers meetings in Las Vegas may occasion the groundwork for all those deals.

Will a lackluster free agent class mean more headline-grabbing trades? That may indeed be answered in the affirmative this winter. Yes, the CBA uncertainty will have a bearing on trades, especially those that involve the assumption of major salary obligations, but big trades still figure to be a prominent part of this offseason.

It's of course impossible to know who's going to be dealt ahead of time, but some big names perhaps on the move this winter include Francisco Lindor, Mason Miller, Spencer Strider, Hunter Greene, Otto Lopez, Jeremy Peña, Ketel Marte, Jacob deGrom, and of course others. Paul Skenes? Almost certainly not, but you'll just as certainly hear his name bandied about.

Turning back to last lockout, it was mostly minor trades before the sport shut down. Yes, we'll see big ones this time around, but they may not happen until we have a new CBA in place and the lockout is over.

Let's make time for the losers, shall we? The teams that didn't make the postseason in 2026 and otherwise qualify will take part in the draft lottery, which is presently scheduled for Dec. 8. That lottery will determine which teams get the top six picks in the 2027 MLB Draft.

This year, 16 of the 18 non-playoff teams will be in the lottery. Non-playoff teams can be barred from the lottery if they've had lottery picks in two consecutive seasons. If a team is a revenue-sharing payor, then it can't be in the lottery in consecutive years. Those wrinkles this year mean that the San Francisco Giants and Pittsburgh Pirates will not be in the lottery and can't pick higher than 10th in the 2027 Draft.

#2650. Borussia Dortmund vs. SV Elversberg preview: Contrasting styles sets up epic clash

With the final international break of 2027 just around the corner, Borussia Dortmund will be keen to go into the imposed rest on a high this weekend. On Saturday afternoon at 15:30 CET, they await the arrival of a newly promoted outfit SV Elversberg on Matchday 9.

Dortmund managed to use last weekend's impressive 2-2 stalemate away to Bayern Munich in their favour midweek. A dominant yet momentarily jittery performance enabled them to defeat Real Betis on a 2-1 scoreline in Wednesday's Champions League encounter.

The result appeared to come at a slight cost, however, for Niko Kovač's troops. Serhou Guirassy hobbled off, leaving him as a doubt for Saturday. Nonetheless, Fábio Silva will be ready to deputise having bagged yet another goal against their Andalusian opponents.

Perhaps even more confidence-building is the fact Kostas Karetsas also scored. The Greek talent has been blighted by injuries, but opening the account will likely give his belief a major boost. BVB's solid rearguard also remains the best in the league, leaking just six.

Serhou Guirassy (strain) could be fit in time, likewise Marcel Sabitzer (illness). Emre Can and Giannis Konstantelias (both ACL tears) naturally won't feature, while Justin Lerma (muscle injury) is expected to remain out.

As for the visitors, this is uncharted territory for SV Elversberg. They ride into town where they will get a taste of one of the Bundesliga's finest footballing temples. The biggest task thereafter is becoming quickly acclimatised to the atmosphere that often unnerves sides.

It's no surprise that this is the first meeting of these two club's in Germany's topflight. The Saarland outfit's meteoric rise up the divisions presents an exciting clash. In ways, it's like a throwback given the visitors play a style akin to Jürgen Klopp's heavy metal era at BVB.

A lot of that credit has to go to coach Vincent Wagner who, along with the Elversberg's chiefs, said they will show no fear and go after teams. That toe-to-toe battling style may just be exactly what could catch Dortmund cold on Saturday if they can make a fast start.

Form has been somewhat turbulent in recent weeks for Elversberg. A crushing DFB-Pokal exit to SV Darmstadt (2-0) and thumping loss to RB Leipzig (4-0) left scars. Fortunately, they bounced back with a barnstorming 4-1 victory over Mainz to settle the nerves last Friday.

Elversberg have a relatively clean bill of health aside from Jan Gyamerah (muscle), Luis Seifert (ligament tear), Tom Zimmerscheid (ankle) and Noah Darvich (muscular problems) who are all due to miss this game.

#2649. How Victor Wembanyama's improved shot diet is leading him to historic heights

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After Victor Wembanyama authored the worst shooting game of his career on opening night, a 1-for-13 showing in a loss to the Thunder, I wrote that the Spurs' honeymoon was over. It was dramatic by design -- a play on the early-season, and in this case single-game, overreactions we always get at the start of every new campaign.

But there was truth in it. Last year, everything the Spurs did was on house money. Winning 62 games. Eliminating the defending champion Thunder on the road in Game 7 of the conference finals. Holding the lead vs. the Knicks for 72% of total minutes played in the Finals. Wembanyama unanimously winning Defensive Player of the Year and finishing third in MVP voting. All prologue, no expectations.

This year, the real story starts, and we knew the benefit of the doubt would be gone. When Wembanyama laid that opening-night egg, the chatter started. He was crowned too soon. He doesn't have a go-to shot or spot. After that game, Wembanyama had no need for the critics. He was his own biggest critic, lamenting his hesitancy and overthinking, saying he needed to "go back to playing the basketball I like."

"I got no reason to be hesitant, no reason to not be myself," Wembanyama said. "For me, it's as simple as that. I'm good when I have fun."

Suffice it to say, he's been having plenty of fun since. Over his last seven games, Wembanyama is averaging 31.4 points, 12.2 rebounds and 4.3 blocks on 52% shooting. After opening 0-2, San Antonio has won six straight, with the latest being Wednesday night's 112-111 thriller over the Mavericks, who erased a 19-point deficit to tie the game with under two minutes to play.

In the end, Wembanyama was just too much. He scored the Spurs' final seven points and 11 of their last 13 and hit the game-winning free-throw. When it was all said and done, the box score read like something out of a video game: 52 points, 24 rebounds and eight blocks as he became the first player to hit those marks since Bob McAdoo more than a half century ago.

CAREER NIGHT FOR VICTOR WEMBANYAMA 🚨🤯 52 PTS (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 24 REB (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 8 BLKFIRST PLAYER WITH 50+ PTS, 20+ REB, 5+ BLK SINCE BOB MCADOO IN 1974. pic.twitter.com/lHzUhYYSTz

Actually, that's selling Wembanyama short. McAdoo only had seven blocks in that 1974 game against the Celtics. Filter it for at least 50, 20 and eight blocks, and only Wilt Chamberlain has done it, and that was before blocks became an official stat. The dude had 29, 15 and five in the first half, for crying out loud. No player in the last 30 years has registered that halftime line.

OK, so Wembanyama is a beast. We all knew this. He's going to have a lot of historic-number games. But what's interesting about the anatomy of this one is where the production came from on the floor, which has quietly been the story of his season.

Wembanyama's shot diet became one of the seminal stories of last year's postseason. He's a relatively random player on the offensive end, and there were stretches when his ability to dance on the perimeter and shoot from range was becoming too easy of a crutch. He's a fine shooter and has a capable handle; for his size, he's extraordinary. But when the listed 7-foot-4 guy who is probably closer to 7-foot-6 is camping out around the 3-point line, it's a win for the defense, particularly at scale.

We saw both sides of this dynamic throughout the playoffs as Wembanyama waffled between a perimeter- and paint-based structure almost from game to game. We saw it against Minnesota in the second round. We saw it again against Oklahoma City in the conference finals when Wembanyama dominated Game 1 at the rim only to be literally pushed out to the perimeter in the following games by Isaiah Hartenstein.

Over the first two games of the Finals, Wembanyama took more shots from outside the paint (22) than he did inside (20), a win for the Knicks, who went up 2-0. In Game 3, he flipped the script, taking 13 of his 18 shots from inside the paint as the Spurs won in a blowout.

There won't always be a direct correlation between Wembanyama's shot diet and the Spurs' outcomes; they're going to win most of their games on sheer talent, and Wembanyama is going to pile up massive numbers for the same reason. But the details matter at the highest level, and so far this season Wembanyama is operating closer to the hoop with greater intention.

Through these first eight games, Wembanyama is taking five more shots a night than he did last year. Nearly all of them are coming from inside the paint, as you can see in the table below highlighting his field-goal attempts from each area.

As a matter of percentage, Wembanyama is taking 42% of his shots from inside three feet this year, up from 33% last year. Those 5.1 dunks per game put him on pace for more than 400 this season, which would obliterate Rudy Gobert's NBA record of 302.

How is Wembanyama doing this? It's not a traditional thing where he's just posting up lower (which he isn't yet strong enough to do on demand and may not ever be), and there still isn't a specific spot or shot he is establishing as the go-to move everyone is clamoring for. It's just the intent to get down there, whether it's by rim rolls, crashing the offensive glass, or forgoing some of the settle 3-pointers for show-and-go drives.

Look at the clip below. He could've taken this initial 3, but he didn't. Instead, he got off the ball to establish himself 10 feet closer to the hoop, where he's now one cut away from a dunk as the Spurs have five 3-point threats on the floor who have collectively pulled every defender away from the basket.

Stephon Castle ⬆️ Victor Wembanyama 👽🤝🏰#NBAHighlights pic.twitter.com/NUX2JAQQ3G

That is what a concerted effort looks like. The seas may not always part like that, but Wembanyama is making it a point to occupy lower positioning more often, where he's ready and able to strike when the slightest crack presents itself. In many cases, Wembanyama is just hanging out beneath the basket or in the dunker's spot along the baseline from the start, rather than having to fight down there after he's started the possession 30 feet away.

One thing the Spurs are doing is initiating pick-and-rolls lower on the floor, so that Wembanyama, with his length, is a single turn from the front of the rim rather than having to navigate all the way from the 3-point line, which gives defenses time to clog his path.

HE'S GOT 47 PTS! 📺 ESPN, @DAZN, @CW35SA pic.twitter.com/ck0iYgngLs

This isn't rocket science. Wembanyama can go up so much higher than everyone else that it's simply a matter of him being near the rim. From there, the Spurs are just throwing it up as you would to an adult playing with kids.

Where Wemby catches the ball for this alley oop is ABSURD pic.twitter.com/azoeaeWUyv

Even the off-the-backboard lobs that Wembanyama is throwing to himself are more than a social media highlight. Note where he's catching the ball: at the free-throw line. When Wembanyama is one step from the rim, just about anything is at his disposal.

WEMBY IS SCARY 😧 pic.twitter.com/A4tPuDvQoa

De'Aaron Fox has talked about running these pick-and-rolls with Wembanyama where he's popping into the free-throw area for soft-spot jumpers, which are going to be there any time he wants as defenses sag back in an attempt, to whatever degree possible, to discourage dunks.

Those shots are about as close to a guaranteed clean look that Wembanyama can get from inside the arc. They are not going in at the moment. He's just 28% from 10-16 feet. But these are the stations from which he can play entirely on his terms. The 3-pointers, particularly the pull-up ones, are on the defense's terms, though he can make them and on plenty of nights will.

So far this year, Wembanyama is making just 24% of his 3s. That will go up, and the threat of him making that shot serves San Antonio's spacing well. He shouldn't, and won't, quit taking them. When they start going in, it could get flat-out unstoppable. But it's a fine balance, and Wembanyama is rightfully erring more on the lower side of the floor this year.

When Wembanyama scored his previous career high of 50 points in 2024, he did so on the strength of eight made 3s. On Wednesday, he only made one 3, while making 15 of his 20 shots from inside the arc. By aggressively going into the paint, he's also in position to draw more fouls, and indeed he made 19 free throws against the Mavs.

That is old-school center stuff. Just flat-out dominating inside. Wembanyama can obviously get buckets either way, but the closer-to-the-hoop way is the better bet all things being equal. On some level, this is pretty simple for a player this size, and you can see Wembanyama starting to figure that out.

#2647. Patriots' TreVeyon Henderson provides update on 'unknown and unexplainable' illness

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson has been out since last week with what the Patriots listed on their injury report as an illness. He missed the team's Week 8 game against the Miami Dolphins and has been out of practice this week.

On Friday morning, Henderson provided an update on his status with a post on Twitter. The statement reads as follows:

I would like to provide an official statement regarding the medical condition I've been experiencing.

Recently, I experienced an unexpected and unusual medical emergency involving a series of unexplained neurological symptoms that required hospitalization for several days. During that time, I underwent extensive medical testing and evaluation. While the results of my comprehensive medical testing have come back positive and reassuring, the cause of this remains unknown and unexplainable.

I will continue working closely with specialists and physical therapists to focus on my recovery, as these symptoms have affected my strength, coordination, and some of my physical functions. I am committed to doing everything necessary to return to full health. My health and long-term well-being remain my foremost priorities.

I want to thank my wife for being by my side through all of this. I want to thank Jesus for giving me a peace that surpasses all understanding. Despite all of this, my heart rejoices in The Lord and my heart is at peace knowing that He is always faithful and His promise of Romans 8:28 always remain true. "And we know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are the called according to His purpose." The purpose of trials in life is not to drive us away from God, but to only bring us closer. May God's Will be done, not mine.

Henderson will presumably be out for the foreseeable future. His health and recovery are obviously of the utmost importance, and it is hard to see him returning to the field unless and until he and his doctors can figure out the cause of his symptoms and how to address them.

Henderson rushed 52 times for 203 yards and a touchdown this season, and added five catches for 45 scoreless yards. During his rookie season a year ago, he totaled 1,132 yards from scrimmage and 10 touchdowns after being selected near the top of the second round in the 2025 NFL Draft.

In his absence, the Patriots will continue to lean on Rhamondre Stevenson as their lead back, with Corey Kiner and Lan Larison working in behind him. They face the Green Bay Packers andDetroit Lions over the next two weeks before taking their bye and then closing out the year with games against the Los Angeles Chargers, Buffalo Bills, Minnesota Vikings, Kansas City Chiefs, New York Jets, Denver Broncos and Dolphins.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Thursday's hot stove happenings.

The Phillies will seek a left-handed setup man this offseason, reports The Athletic. Philadelphia has Tanner Banks and Tim Mayza, though both are middle-innings lefties more than high-leverage relievers. Manager Don Mattingly's late-inning unit is all righties at the moment: Jonathan Bowlan, Caleb Kilian, Jhoan Duran, and Alex McFarlane.

We ranked four lefty relievers among our top 50 free agents: Adrian Morejon (No. 2), JoJo Romero (No. 31), Alex Vesia (No. 35), and Kris Bubic (No. 45). Morejon and Bubic may get opportunities to start next season. Other free agent lefties include Tim Hill, A.J. MInter, Sean Newcomb, Steven Okert, AJ Puk, and former Phillie Gregory Soto.

The Yankees need almost an entirely new bullpen this offseason, and they have interest in re-signing setup man Paul Blackburn, according to the New York Daily News. New York tendered closer David Bednar the $23.15 million qualifying offer and seems likely to get him back, either on the QO or on a multi-year deal, but they will need to improve the setup crew regardless.

We ranked Blackburn as the No. 33 free agent this offseason. He had a terrific season with the Yankees in 2026, his first year as a full-time reliever. The Yankees have shown the ability to drum up quality relievers almost out of nowhere. They tend to let those guys leave as free agents, then build up someone else to replace them. This happened when Blackburn replaced Luke Weaver.

Among their list of wants this offseason, the Marlins will look to add to their rotation and bullpen, as well as a corner bat, reports the Miami Herald. That corner bat could be at first base, third base, left or right fields. Sandy Alcantara and Eury Pérez are the only locks for Miami's rotation, though Max Meyer should be ready to go next season following this year's neck injury.

Gold Glove finalist Javier Sanoja filled in at third base capably this year, though he fits best as a super utility man who plays all over. Owen Caissie, Griffin Conine, and Heriberto Hernández are Miami's corner outfield options, and Kyle Stowers moved from the outfield to first base in 2026. There are opportunities to improve aplenty for the Marlins.

#2644. Mjällby AIF: An Analysis of the Swedish Champions’ Possession Play – MH

von Next Generation am 23.12.2025 in den Kategorien Team Portraits mit 1 Kommentar

Mjällby AIF are Swedish champions. For the first time in their history, the small fishing village of 1,300 inhabitants has managed to outperform the competition from the bigger cities, helped by an exceptional brand of attacking football.

“Europe’s surprise team comes from a tiny fishing village on Sweden’s southern coast. The sporting director is a farmer. The coach is a former school principal. The story of Mjällby AIF: a miracle?“ – Dorfklub Mjällby AIF mischt Schweden auf: Einsame Spitze – 11FREUNDE

”A unique tale in football: In Sweden, Mjällby AIF from a small fishing village and with little money are celebrating the championship, thanks in part to the football doctor.“ – Mjällby AIF: Der Meister aus dem Fischerdorf | DIE ZEIT

“Not even ten years ago, the village club stood on the brink of collapse. This weekend, Mjällby could become the smallest place ever to produce a European champion.“ – Mjällby könnte Meister werden: Bekommt Schweden einen Sensationsmeister – 11FREUNDE

“Always follow the beach, then turn left at the campsite. Anyone heading for the stadium of league leaders Mjällby AIF in the Swedish fishing village of Hällevik won’t struggle to find it. ‘We play where the world ends and the sea begins’ is how the club describes the route to their home ground that bears the lovely name Strandvallen.“ – Fußball: Warum der Dorfklub Mjällby AIF Meister in Schweden werden könnte | sportschau.de

“For Mjällby’s opponents, a trip to the far south of Sweden feels like a journey to the Earth’s end. ‘When teams come on here on the bus they drive and drive, through the farms, past the fishing harbours,’ says Hasse Larsson. ‘They keep driving and then, when they can’t drive any further, they find our stadium.’” – Mjällby making minor miracles in an extraordinary Swedish football story | European club football | The Guardian

“’It’s 1,500 inhabitants in the village where they play, and you’re just flabbergasted when you see this elite football going on,’ Erik Hadzic – a reporter for TV4 Fotbollskanalen, who has covered the team for the last five years – tells CNN Sports. ‘Mjällby winning the Swedish championship is arguably the biggest sensation in the history of the Swedish league.’ The tiny team from Hällevik has not just won the league, either. It has absolutely blown away the competition.” – Mjällby AIF: How a tiny Swedish team achieved one of the biggest ever shocks in European soccer | CNN

Mjällby AIF have managed to appear across virtually every media outlet. By winning the Swedish championship, the small village club now enter Champions League qualifying, giving them the chance to measure themselves against the very biggest. This article aims to explain the type of football that led Mjällby to the Swedish title. Since their possession game stands out, the analysis focuses exclusively on this aspect.

Assistant coach Dr Karl Marius Aksum is regarded as the main architect of Mjällby’s attacking football. In his doctoral thesis, he wrote about visual perception and more specifically about scanning in professional footballers. Scanning is defined there as “all head movements away from the ball with the intention of gathering performance related information from one’s surroundings.” Aksum uses Gibson’s ecological theory of perception to show why scanning matters.

This theory emphasises that perception is inseparable from action possibilities. Humans do not only perceive objects, but above all the possibilities for action that an environment offers them, known as affordances. Translated into a football context: only when a player recognises the relevant elements of a situation, such as an opponent’s position, a passing option or a teammate’s run, can he make the appropriate decision. If such action possibilities remain unnoticed due to poor scanning, they will not be used.

Unlike most previous research on scanning in football, Aksum equipped players with specialised sports goggles using eye tracking technology, collecting data during full sided eleven versus eleven matches. These game realistic data allowed him to obtain results that reflect actual match conditions far more closely. The findings show that an average scan lasts roughly 0.40 seconds, although the most common scan duration is substantially shorter at 0.26 seconds. Moreover, 90.3 percent of all scans are shorter than 0.66 seconds. Fixations occur only rarely, as just 2.3 percent of scans contain a fixation and these last significantly longer than regular scans.

It is also highlighted that players do not process details such as faces in this short time frame, but mainly detect movements and colours. For training practice, this means that drills requiring prolonged or detailed information gathering during scanning lack match realism. In game situations, the brief duration of scans only allows players to pick up fundamental spatial and colour based cues. I have linked the dissertation here, titled ”Visual Perception in Elite Football“. The topic of scanning will also be examined in greater detail in another future article, possibly in a slightly different format.

Before Aksum’s arrival two years ago, Mjällby struggled heavily to turn matches around after falling behind. The club subsequently advertised a position aimed at solving this issue and succeeded. Karl Marius Aksum has since been appointed head coach for the 2026 season, taking over from the highly capable leader Anders Torstensson, who has moved into the role of technical director. Mjällby are now able to play through high pressing opponents as well as create chances against deep defensive blocks.

To conduct this analysis, I examined six different matches. Since six games are a limited sample and could skew certain aspects of the possession game, I list them here: Mjällby 4-1 Degerfors, AIK 2-1 Mjällby, Norrköpping 1-1 Mjällby, Mjällby 2-0 AIK, Malmö 1-3 Mjällby, Mjällby 2-0 Elfsborg.

The selection of matches was not made by me but by the aforementioned Karl Marius Aksum. I am therefore confident that these six fixtures cover the majority of Mjällby’s overall game. Many thanks once again for the openness. Obtaining suitable video material from the Allsvenskan turned out to be far more difficult than expected.

Mjällby generally operate in a nominal 1-3-2-4-1 structure. Goalkeeper Törnqvist is exceptionally strong with the ball at his feet. He is therefore consistently integrated into Mjällby’s build-up through a goalkeeper line. When Mjällby build with a back four, he can function as either the right or the left centre back. He very often looks for line breaking passes through the middle. His qualities have also caught the attention of Como, currently fifth in Serie A as of December 2025, who have already signed him. Como under coach Cesc Fàbregas also repeatedly build short with the goalkeeper involved.

The back three usually consists of right centre back Iqbal, central centre back Norén and left centre back Pettersson. Iqbal in particular pushed higher in certain matches during the build-up phase. Despite standing 1.92 metres tall, he is technically excellent and can therefore also take on the slightly higher and wider full back role of a back four depending on the opponent. Against deep defensive blocks, both outside centre backs of the back three are actively involved in the attacking phase. More on this later.

The wing backs in the five man line are Johansson on the right and Stroud on the left. Johansson is one of the more experienced players at 28 and among those with the most minutes. He frequently provides depth with runs beyond the opposition back line, combining pace with physical strength. He is also the first Mjällby player ever to be capped for the Swedish national team. Left wing back Stroud, on the other hand, was deployed centrally as a number ten towards the end of the season. Left wing back Stavitski is considered the primary replacement. The wing backs can operate at virtually any height and are used asymmetrically depending on the opponent. They often provide width when Mjällby attack with two wide players.

The centre of Mjällby’s structure is something of a holy grail in their build-up. In the nominal 1-3-2-4-1, it consists of two tens and two sixes, but only nominally. To gain a clearer understanding of Mjällby’s build-up, I eventually began to describe the structures as for example 1-3-diamond-w2-d1 (w=wide, d=deep), 4-trapezoid-1-w2, 1-3-Y-2-d1 and so on. By isolating the centre as a separate perspective, the different central configurations become particularly visible. Depending on build-up height and the opponent, Mjällby vary the number and positioning of their tens, eights and sixes. What stays constant is that there are always four central players. The w2 notation (w=wide) refers to the wing backs, though not perfectly accurate since they can also abandon the wide corridor.

Six Gustavsson is essentially always part of the central unit. He plays from the deepest central role, close to the defensive line, and is the team’s captain. Until his departure in the summer, the technically gifted six or eight Rojkjaer was also a constant. He was replaced depending on the opponent by various players, such as eight Thorell, left wing back Stroud or ten Kjaer. On the right side as a ten or eight, Gustafson (not to be confused with six Gustavsson) usually features.

The left or central ten Manneh deserves special mention, as he brings exceptional qualities. He is explosive, very fast and excellent when driving forward on the dribble. Alongside wing back Johansson, Manneh regularly provides depth or beats opponents to create superiority. He is already being linked with clubs from the top two divisions in England. His output is all the more remarkable considering that Mjällby as a team rank lowest in the league for dribbles. Dribbling simply is not a frequently used attacking tool for them, yet Manneh consistently stands out.

Up front, the lone striker is usually the experienced Bergström. He is used as a target and is frequently the focal point in the build-up, laying balls off for advancing central players. On aerial deliveries, he is the primary target.

Mjällby’s possession game is not the only factor behind the Swedish champions’ success. Naturally, their play also includes several other interesting elements, such as ball-near overloads during opposition throw-ins or a strong central focus in their pressing. In attack, they also make frequent use of long throw-ins into the box, and set pieces play an important role. The possession game, however, is one of the most intriguing in Europe, as it operates with completely different structures and patterns than usual. Accordingly, the focus of this team analysis lies on this aspect.

Mjällby’s build-up structure varies significantly depending on the opponent’s pressing approach. This naturally creates challenges for the analysis. While there are overarching principles, these do not lead to fixed or repetitive patterns. On the contrary, Mjällby’s build-up looks particularly different when facing a high press or full man marking on goal kicks. The main differences arise from the structures and target zones Mjällby uses to exploit specific weaknesses in the opponent’s pressing. For this reason, the following analysis of the build-up will be broken down by match.

Mjällby started, as usual, from a 3-2-4-1. There was, however, an important detail in the central area. With Bang-Kittilsen and Manneh, two natural number 10s were fielded, meaning that Gustafson – another 10/8 profile – occupied the nominal holding midfielder role. Depending on the phase of play, Mjällby could therefore rely on three number 10s and build from a one-three structure in midfield.

Degerfors pressed in a 5-4-1, shifting into a 5-2-3 during the high press. As is common in the Swedish league, they avoided full man marking and instead maintained a plus-one or plus-two advantage in the last line. Consequently, Degerfors did not press goalkeeper Törnqvist directly, but triggered their press after the first pass. Because both Degerfors midfielders pushed high to avoid being outnumbered centrally, a large space opened between their midfield and defensive line. In addition, the half backs in the Degerfors back three did not step forward into this space but held their position on the last line to provide cover.

Mjällby build up from a 4-trapezoid-3 structure and look to transition into three number tens in order to exploit the large space between the lines in Degerfors’ 5-4-1 pressing shape.

Mjällby’s obvious objective was therefore to exploit this large space between the lines. Using the goalkeeper as an extra player and with three number 10s available, they were well equipped to access and run through that zone. The starting point for the build-up against Degerfors was the 4-trapezoid-3. Fullbacks Stroud and Johansson pushed up to the level of striker Bergström, engaging the wingbacks of the opposition’s back five.

A typical feature of Mjällby’s build-up against a more passive high press or high block is their narrow four-man first line. The two outer centre backs spread roughly to the width of the penalty-area edges. The central centre back (usually on the left) and the goalkeeper (usually on the right) form the inner pair of this line. The extreme narrowness of this four-man row is notable. While many top European teams build with a slightly wider back three, Mjällby positions four players in a tight horizontal line.

The aim, beyond achieving numerical superiority, is likely to enable passing routes around the pressing block. Through the flat and narrow positions of the nominal fullbacks in the first line and the high positioning of Johansson and Stroud, the entire wing channel is opened. Typically, one of the central midfielders drops into that space to become available. The passing angle into the wide channel is optimal because the dropping player does not need to move all the way toward the touchline. Instead, he can remain closer to the centre, with shorter distances and better conditions to play back inside.

Due to the narrow back four in the build-up and the high positioning of the full-backs, the number tens can receive the ball around the block without having to drop all the way out to the touchline.

The heart of the build-up in this match lay in the central area. The basic structure was a trapezoid shape with the initially narrower positions of the sixes, Gustafson and Gustavsson, and the slightly wider starting points of the 10s, Bang-Kittilsen and Manneh. To continuously generate new passing options, Gustafson, Bang-Kittilsen and Manneh constantly searched for fresh open lanes and spaces to position themselves in. Initially, Gustafson often pushed deep into the large space between the lines, which prompted the two other 10s to adjust and occupy alternative passing lanes. This created constant rotation and caused problems for Degerfors.

From Degerfors’ perspective, they were outnumbered centrally against Mjällby’s four central players. When one of the 10s attacked a lane through the pressing block, another central player reacted by creating a passing option around the block. By dropping and offering an outlet outside the pressing trap, Degerfors faced a dilemma. If they closed the passing lane to the dropping midfielder, they opened a new channel through the centre. As a result, Mjällby repeatedly managed to open new passing routes and break the press through the rotating midfielders. The same logic applied in their build-up against Degerfors’ mid block, which will be examined again in that section, this time supported with an additional graphic.

Mjällby operated in this match primarily from a 3-diamond-w2-d1 structure. The diamond in midfield was formed by captain Gustavsson as the six, Rojkjaer (a six in the 3-4-2-1) as the left eight, Gustafson (a ten in the 3-4-2-1) as the right eight, and Manneh as the ten. In contrast to the match against Degerfors, the fullbacks Stroud and Johansson were not supposed to remain permanently on the height of the last line. Instead, they dropped towards the ball on the outside lane especially when AIK managed to put pressure on the outer centre back in the build-up. As a general rule, Mjällby’s fullbacks act as the width providers in the build-up against a high-pressing opponent.

AIK used pure man marking in both the high press and on goal kicks. Unlike Mjällby’s other opponents, AIK did not maintain a plus-one in the last line. Instead, one of their centre backs directly engaged ten Manneh. In addition, AIK’s defenders repeatedly pushed forward aggressively from behind onto the Mjällby midfielders in a man-marking manner to prevent any free player from emerging. This had the major advantage of not having to press in numerical inferiority in the centre.

However, Mjällby managed particularly in the first 15 minutes to escape the man marking through a flat build-up. To achieve this, Mjällby used very flat eights and a ball-near fullback dropping towards the play. This created a kind of 5(GK)-3-1-2 structure, with one high fullback acting as the far-side striker and the other fullback staying flat as the ball-near option. The space between the lines was opened, with only ten Manneh positioned there, allowing him to exploit his strengths in larger spaces.

Mjällby’s 4-3-1-1-w2 with asymmetrical full-backs against AIK’s man-oriented marking: by creating an overload behind his direct opponent, Rojkjaer forces one of AIK’s centre-backs to loosen the man-marking on Manneh in order to provide cover, which makes Manneh available to receive the ball.

Mjällby succeeded in the early phases whenever they managed to “loosen” the man marking of the AIK centre back on Manneh. For example, eight Rojkjaer ran into the expanded space between the lines behind his direct opponent. Because this created a brief numerical inferiority for AIK, their marking centre back instinctively dropped off, allowing Manneh to be found as the free player between the lines. In general, Mjällby aimed in the build-up to open the centre in order to find the passing lane from a building defender into Manneh between the lines or into Bergström on the last line.

The fundamental objective of Mjällby’s build-up is to find the free player and then switch to the far side. If possible, this is done diagonally through the centre. Against man marking, however, Mjällby naturally encounters problems. Especially after Mjällby’s 1–0 goal in the 10th minute, AIK increased their risk-taking and applied tighter and earlier man marking. Because Mjällby’s build-up relies on freeing the central free player through coordinated movements, they struggle against pure man marking, in which no such free player appears. This theme runs throughout the entire analysis of their build-up against high pressing and becomes particularly relevant after taking the lead, since opponents then tend to abandon their cover and their plus-one advantage in the last line.

Of course, Mjällby also has mechanisms against pure man marking. Against AIK, a clear 5-3-1-2 structure appeared in goal-kick situations. Right back Johansson dropped very deep, while left back Stroud moved into the centre and high into the second-striker line. The idea behind this recurring goal-kick structure was to force the opponent either into a 3-versus-3 without cover or to abandon their man marking and instead pull an additional covering player backwards.

Mjällby’s 5-3-1-2 with asymmetrical wing-backs against AIK’s man-oriented marking at goal kicks: counter-movements in the front line and a counter-pressing net created by supporting runners stepping up.

Because AIK chose pure man marking without a covering player when full man marking the goal kick, Mjällby often went long to one of the three advanced players, frequently fullback Stroud, who dropped into the opened wide channel and laid the ball off to the players running through. The runners (the three midfielders and the ball-near fullback from the 5-3 structure) tried both to create lay-off options and to form a counterpressing net to win second balls. It is generally noticeable that Mjällby, due to their strong central occupation in the build-up against high pressing, wins a large number of second balls after turnovers. This is also a key part of Mjällby’s build-up play.

At the same time, Mjällby prepared the long balls on goal kicks through opposite movements of the three forward players. Before the ball was played, they made horizontal opposite runs to loosen the man marking and to gain more space and time on the lay-off.

It is also noticeable that the tighter the opponent moves into man marking, the more frequently striker Bergström is used as a target player. Whenever Mjällby came under pressure, the ball was often played into Bergström, who with his back to goal could hold the ball and lay it off to the midfielders running beyond him. Mjällby repeatedly managed through the movements of their midfielders to open the central passing lane or the direct ball into striker Bergström. Against AIK, Bergström was often found diagonally by Johansson, the flat fullback, from the touchline, or directly through a flat throw from goalkeeper Törnqvist. Bergström also served as an additional target player on goal kicks alongside fullback or striker Stroud.

As the nominal holding midfielder Rojkjaer transferred to Danish top-flight club Nordsjaelland during the summer transfer window, he was replaced by number eight Thorell in the return match against AIK. Due to weather conditions, the Allsvenskan pauses during winter and is played throughout the summer, meaning departures can occur mid-season. On the left side of the back three, Pettersson started instead of Iqbal, maintaining the same role and positional profile. In attack, Johansson started in place of the usual first-choice striker Bergström.

In contrast to the first leg against AIK, Mjällby used a slightly different central structure. As left-sided eight Thorell positioned himself higher than six Gustavsson, and right-sided ten Gustafson operated even higher than Thorell, this shape can be described neither as a diamond nor as a trapezoid. The most accurate description is a “Y-structure”. This highly interesting structure consists of Thorell and Gustavsson staggered vertically and slightly horizontally, supported by two tens.

Due to the staggered positioning of the two number sixes, a kind of diagonal “Y” shape emerges in central areas. From this structure, a variety of counter-movements with changes of vertical levels can be created, which are particularly difficult to defend against in a man-oriented marking scheme.

The Y-structure offers several advantages, particularly against man marking. Crucially, the Y is not fully symmetrical in its initial positioning. Because Thorell as an eight always started slightly offset from six Gustavsson, he formed a diagonal either with the left or the right ten. From this diagonal, it becomes significantly easier to generate varied horizontal opposite movements combined with changes of level. These movements are especially difficult to defend in a man-marking system, as they disrupt the opponent’s structure and greatly extend pressing distances. Defensive handovers also become much more difficult, since the diagonal Y allows for a wide range of possible opposite movements with level changes.

The diagonal Y also provides additional advantages against non-man-marking pressing. From this structure, the build-up players can quickly occupy a variety of passing lanes, and central access can be opened through easily created lateral overloads. The shape is also beneficial for lay-off play. Because multiple vertical levels are occupied simultaneously, simple movements can create several different lay-off options. The vertical staggering also improves counterpressing, as immediate mutual cover is available in transition moments.

As a result, a wide variety of movements could be observed from Mjällby within this Y-structure, making the central organisation appear almost random at times. In particular, eight Thorell could be found in nearly every area of the pitch. It was also helpful that the central players frequently rotated positions and roles among themselves. Since each player interpreted the respective role slightly differently, the build-up became even harder for AIK to read. This allowed Mjällby to progress the ball successfully on numerous occasions. As the first half progressed, AIK were also less frequently able to maintain numerical equality on the last line, which in turn created an extra player in midfield for Mjällby.

In contrast to the first leg, AIK initially defended goal kicks with a plus-one advantage on the last line. On goal kicks, Mjällby attempted to build in a similar way to the first leg, using a 5-3-1-2 or 5-3-3 structure, with left back Stroud positioned more centrally and higher in the forward line, and right back Johansson remaining flat and wide in the five-man build-up line. In this match, however, ten Manneh was much more involved in the opposite movements used to prepare long balls, which explains the shift towards a 5-3-3 instead of a 5-3-1-2. The three forwards moved unpredictably before the long ball, aiming to loosen man marking, remain difficult to access directly, and gain more time and space for lay-offs to the players arriving from deeper positions.

After approximately eight minutes, AIK adjusted their four-versus-three advantage on the last line. From that point on, one of their defenders was ready to step out onto one of Mjällby’s eights. Notably, Mjällby did not immediately choose the long ball from the goalkeeper in response. Instead, they first triggered the press through a short build-up and then played through it. There were several different variants of how the central players could behave in these situations. For example, one side could be overloaded by all three central midfielders, opening a diagonal passing lane to the far side towards striker or ten Manneh.

Around the 55th minute, a successfully executed goal kick from the asymmetrical 5-3-3 structure led to a free kick, which subsequently resulted in Mjällby’s 1–0 goal. First, the press was triggered by two passes between the goalkeeper and a centre back. From the opposite movements of the forwards, two attackers dropped towards the ball while one ran in behind. One of the forwards, in this case Manneh, was found directly with a flat diagonal pass into this lane, allowing him to turn and access the far side around fullback Johansson. As I cannot provide the video material on this page for legal reasons, I have linked the sequence as a video on X:
