#2631. NBA relegation zone predictions: Ranking the 7 worst teams in the race to avoid the bottom of the standings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When the NBA reformed the draft lottery, it did so with the hopes that all 30 teams would be somewhat competitive. But two weeks into the 2026-27 season, that isn't proving true.

Five teams have just a single win so far this season, and in many cases, those wins are only coming when they play one another. The Los Angeles Clippers have only beaten the Sacramento Kings. The Chicago Bulls have only beaten the Milwaukee Bucks. The Kings' only win came when the Dallas Mavericks rested Kyrie Irving.

No matter how the incentive structures are designed, the NBA will always have a handful of very bad teams. Some teams are poorly run. Some teams are besieged by injuries. Some teams are simply in transitional stages of their roster builds. The old NBA was designed to make bad teams good quickly. The new one is designed to make it harder for teams to bounce back from the bottom.

As part of last spring's lottery reform, the three worst teams in the league are now punished for losing. In the new 3-2-1 lottery format, the seven best teams to miss the Play-In Tournament get three lottery balls each out of the 37 available ones, while the three worst teams each get only two. In theory, that should create an all-out war to avoid the bottom three. In practice, well, we'll get into that shortly.

For now, as the bottom of the league is starting to take shape, let's take a look at our relegation zone candidates. While injuries could certainly create more of them as we go, seven teams stand out as reasonable threats for a bottom-three record so far this season. We're going to rank them from least to most likely to land in the relegation zone, with the top three teams being our official picks to take that lottery hit in May.

Remember, this is not merely a ranking of the NBA's worst teams. It's who is likeliest to land in the bottom three of the standings, a necessary distinction for reasons you're about to find out.

There isn't a more dumbfounding team to watch in the NBA right now than the Jazz. For four years, Utah was a smart, well-run team that lost because the front office did everything in its power to deprive its coach of talent. Well, coach Will Hardy is allowed to win now. It just isn't happening.

The inventive, flowing offense of years past is sputtering. No. 2 overall pick Darryn Peterson isn't making jumpers and can't get to the rim. Players needed for size and defense -- like Josh Okogie and Jaxson Hayes -- are killing the offense. Everything is running through Keyonte George because he's the only player on the floor creating consistent advantages. He's not a true point guard, and the lack of passing on the floor right now is palpable. Their lone victory came by a single point at home against the New Orleans Pelicans. Not exactly inspiring.

Any dreams of a 50-win, top-six seed season died with the Walker Kessler trade. This team is screaming for anyone who can screen and rebound. Getting Jusuf Nurkić back will help, and eventually, Jaren Jackson Jr. will take the floor again, too. You'd hope Peterson eventually figures some things out. He's a No. 2 overall pick. He's too talented to struggle this much unless the medical issues that plagued him at Kansas are persisting. There are reasons to believe this will get better. The Jazz should eventually be at least competitive.

But we're barely into November and even their more modest, post-Kessler Play-In ambitions already seem to be on life support. The Western Conference is far deeper than it looked a month ago and the Jazz are digging themselves a hole they're going to struggle to climb out of. This is a bad defensive roster even at full strength, and if the offense is this disjointed, the postseason just isn't on the table. After a four-year tank, that's a real concern in Utah. Even sniffing the relegation zone, given the time spent even getting to this point, is a borderline disaster.

The Suns come in ahead of one-win Utah -- and the two-win Orlando Magic they just beat -- because those teams have more substantial reinforcements incoming. The Suns will benefit greatly from the eventual return of Mark Williams, if only because, at this stage, Khaman Maluach just is not ready to play serious NBA minutes. But Williams isn't, say, Jaren Jackson or Paolo Banchero. Phoenix's problems are internal.

They were the first team of the season to leak displeasure to the press, with Chris Haynes reporting that the locker room is frustrated over the lack of a point guard. There's a fair bit of statistical evidence suggesting the Suns could address that problem by benching Jalen Green for Collin Gillespie. Eventually, Green's performance will force the issue. If your value is derived entirely from scoring and you're averaging 12 points on 41-22-69 shooting splits, you won't be long for anyone's starting lineup.

The bigger problem here is the loss of last year's defense-and-hustle identity. The Suns only just surrendered the NBA's 30th defensive ranking to another team on this list, and their deflections, loose ball recoveries and offensive rebounding are way down. As of this writing, they're the worst rebounding team in the NBA. Many of the players responsible for last year's identity are playing less than they did last year. Green simply isn't a defense and energy player. Neither is Miles Bridges, who they gave up yet another unprotected first-round pick to get.

Devin Booker is slipping. The shotmaking bar on superstar-level value for a guard who never makes plays nor gets to the rim at an elite level is almost impossibly high. He basically has to be a high-volume 3-point shooter making close to 40% of his attempts to justify his supermax deal. He hasn't come close to that in years. He doesn't quite have his old burst, either, and after the Bridges trade, the Suns are down to very few remaining draft assets with which they can improve. There's probably enough talent here that the Suns will eventually be able to eke their way to 30 or so wins, but the early returns here are pretty discouraging.

Here's where we take our first real step down in terms of roster talent. The bottom five teams are simply worse than the remaining 25. There's no All Star-level talent here, like George in Utah or Booker in Phoenix. Michael Porter Jr. made his case a year ago, but his volume is down with Julius Randle on the roster. With the Nets, Randle has been largely inefficient and is turning the ball over more than ever. Only three teams turn the ball over more frequently than they do.

They're attempting to sacrifice high opponent 3-point volume for minimizing attempts at the rim. It's working in terms of volume, but once anyone does get to the rim, they're scoring there with impunity because Brooklyn simply doesn't have a reliable, individual rim protector. They're among the most frequent fouling defenses in the NBA. Last year's No. 8 overall pick, Egor Dëmin, is already hurt and has all but abandoned shooting inside the arc. Young guards, no matter how much promise they show, are usually bad. The goal of this season is to develop several of them. Mikel Brown Jr. and the improving Nolan Traore are years away from what they'll eventually become.

Here's where we really have to start talking about incentives. Brooklyn owes its first-round pick to the Houston Rockets. Now, the Jazz and Suns owe their first-round picks out as well, but under different circumstances. The Suns won't control their own pick again until the actual sun burns out, so what happens to their picks isn't really their concern. The Jazz have picked in the top five two years in a row, so their pick, currently owed to the Memphis Grizzlies, can't land there again, and will therefore have a clean slate next year. But the Nets, who are several years away from winning meaningfully barring something unforeseen, probably want to avoid having their pick land in the top five, as teams are forbidden from ending up there three years in a row, or, in the worst-case scenario, coming in at No. 1, which would bar them from picking there in 2028.

The Nets are, in other words, incentivized to lose, which is exactly what this system was supposed to prevent. Now, they can't go about it as brazenly as tankers of the past have, as commissioner Adam Silver now has expanded powers to punish teams for tanking. But the NBA can't stop them from, say, trading useful veterans like Porter at the deadline. Brooklyn didn't do so a year ago when it should have, so this will be something to watch when February rolls around. If the Nets keep Porter, they're probably good enough to duck the relegation zone. If they move him, well, getting in there may not be the goal, but it would be a potentially helpful byproduct.

Considering the Nets traded for Randle in June, though, it seems as though Brooklyn, to the delight of Houston (which walks away with six lottery balls between Brooklyn and Phoenix in this scenario), intends to try to win. There are possible reasons for that ranging from culture-building to job security, but until the Nets show their hand, we'll leave them out of the bottom three for now.

Here's a sobering thought: of the seven teams we're covering in this space, the Kings are the only one that fits into the relegation zone system as intended. They don't owe their pick out to another team. They aren't on any consecutive high picks clock. They're just a bad team trying to rebuild organically. They want high draft picks, which means they don't want to be in the bottom three.

They might even be willing to trade a small asset to improve at the deadline for this purpose if necessary. If nothing else, they have the salary to do so. Between Zach LaVine and De'Andre Hunter, they have over $70 million in expiring money to dangle if doing so makes sense. Wins tend to be elusive in Sacramento, but the Kings actually want them.

They are unfortunately ill-equipped to get them. The 2026-27 Kings are quite frankly one of the strangest teams ever assembled. Former All-Star Domantas Sabonis is playing 36 minutes a game and attempting fewer shots than Precious Achiuwa. Darius Acuff Jr., meanwhile, has the second-highest usage rate any rookie has posted in NBA history, behind only Joel Embiid. He has higher usage this season than Cade Cunningham and Jalen Brunson.

The Kings aren't playing like a team whose goal is to win. They are playing like a team whose sole goal is to fast-forward through Acuff's developmental curve. That's not a crazy decision given their circumstances, but as we've addressed with Brooklyn, young guards can be productive without being especially helpful when it comes to winning. Acuff is taking shots that players like Brunson and Cunningham spend whole careers earning the right to attempt, and he is understandably far worse at actually converting them. Veteran teammates don't tend to enjoy watching rookies chuck bad shots, and without a good defender in sight, it's not as though the Kings can win on the other end of the floor. They're going to be on the bubble here. We just have three better candidates.

The ball-handling deficit here is bleak. Only the Charlotte Hornets are turning the ball over more, and nobody is even close when it comes to points allowed off turnovers. Considering Darius Garland's perpetual issues staying on the court, things are only going to get harder from here. Getting Brandon Ingram back from his partially torn Achilles will help, but he's much more of an individual shotmaker than someone who can lift an entire offense. They're struggling to generate anything near the rim as well, ranking 24th in paint points thus far. They're defending better than most of this group, a byproduct of Jeff Van Gundy's presence on their bench, but even that is at risk because of those pesky incentive structures.

The Clippers obviously owe their own first-round pick to the Oklahoma City Thunder. That isn't especially relevant, but we should note that the Clippers owe their top-three protected pick to the Philadelphia 76ers in 2029 through swap rights, and they'd probably prefer to avoid starting that top-five clock now because consecutive top-five picks would ensure they have no chance of keeping their 2029 selection.

More importantly, though, the Clippers were just stripped of five first-round picks for circumventing the salary cap. That puts them at an enormous draft capital deficit moving forward. There's no way the Clippers can recoup all of that lost value, but it makes plenty of sense for them to trade veterans for whatever value they can get in the name of setting up their future. Players like Brook Lopez, Kris Dunn, Max Strus, Derrick Jones Jr. and Rui Hachimura are all in their primes and could net positive value back in the right trades.

Since the Clippers have nothing to lose by getting relegated this year, it would likely behoove them to cash in these players for whatever value they get. If they do so, they're going to wind up in pretty rough shape down the stretch.

From a team we know circumvented the cap to a team we think very well might have. The Bucks are currently being investigated for the contract they gave Gary Trent Jr. over the summer. And the fact that he has now been DNP-CD'd in six of Milwaukee's eight games certainly doesn't help their case. If they lose picks, they're incentivized to try to make those up by trading away players they don't intend to keep long-term.

Even as it stands, the Bucks are just a bad team. They're a bottom-five offense and defense with no notable injuries. The roster mix is what you'd expect out of a team that just traded the best player in franchise history without receiving a premium asset in return: a jumbled mess. Half of the roster is comprised of shooting guards. They're thin enough at forward that they're still forced to start Kyle Kuzma, and their $108 million starting center, Myles Turner, is averaging single digits. The young players are years away. The old players are years away from the versions of themselves that warranted the minutes and money they're currently receiving.

None of this is especially surprising. It's the first year of a rebuild, and the Bucks won't control their own pick again until 2031. They're in no rush here, and the Pelicans, who control Milwaukee's pick this year, stand to lose draft value because of it.

The Bulls have been the NBA's worst team this season by a pretty comfortable margin. A brutal early schedule is somewhat to blame, of course, but they have nearly a five-point net rating gap between themselves and the No. 29-ranked Kings. They're a bottom-five defense in terms of both points in the paint allowed per game and 3-pointers made per game.

Only the Clippers give up more points off of turnovers. They rank 27th in rebounding rate. Years of steady scoring growth from Josh Giddey have seemingly been undone in two weeks. Matas Buzelis is both playing and shooting less than he did a year ago. Caleb Wilson is exploring the studio space in all of the messy ways you want a top rookie to do so. They're shooting just over 27% from 3-point range.

So the Bulls have the basketball end of the equation covered... but they also have the incentive side to consider. Remember, Wilson was the No. 4 overall pick in June. That means that another top-five pick in 2027 locks them out of the top five in 2028. The 2027 class is considered historically weak, but 2028 is expected to be stronger. Realistically, the Bulls probably don't expect to be any good next year, either. The last thing they should want is to risk getting stuck with a middling 2028 pick because they land at No. 5 in 2027.

Chicago is already terrible and has good reason to try to stay that way. Wilson has an incredibly bright future, but the present is understandably bleak.

#2630. Essay: Escape – MX

von Next Generation am 06.02.2026 in den Kategorien Opinion mit 3 Kommentaren

A few thoughts and reflections on the analysis bubble.

Humans want to understand. A fundamental need of our species eventually developed a concept for the desire to understand and to derive understanding: analysis. Carried through the centuries and applied primarily in literature, this drive increasingly found its way into the comparative physical activity of humans-sport. It fascinates hundreds of thousands of people every weekend; the urge to comprehend the logic – even where there is none – behind the results has become ever more omnipresent. Yet analysis existed long before people fully understood what analysis was – analyzing no longer becomes analysis simply because one is aware of doing it. Tracing the philosophical origins of analysis, pure analysis is merely a subform of communication: communicating by breaking down a whole into parts.

If we understand analysis as part of a larger communication context, it is hardly surprising that analytical formats in Europe developed primarily through blogs and digital platforms – parallel to the ongoing technologization of the world. Analysis has always existed, but only with the internet did it gain new relevance: communication could, for the first time, reach a potentially unlimited audience permanently. This explains an apparent contradiction of its origins: analysis exists continuously, yet it is always dependent on its recipients. Without an audience, it has no effect. In the words of Niklas Luhmann, communication does not arise from mere sending, but from understanding on the part of the receiver. Analysis is therefore not an isolated act, but an interactive process.

In the age of social media, however, this dependence increasingly leads to a dead end. Highly complex matters are expected to be made understandable, consumable, and entertaining within thirty seconds. Paradoxically, social media produces more recipients than ever – and simultaneously a structural scarcity of attention. Georg Franck refers to this as the “attention economy,” in which visibility, rather than truth or depth, becomes the central currency. For a long time, analysis was a dialogical process: presenting, structuring, weighing – a reciprocal interplay between sender and receiver, reliant on resonance and reflection. Jürgen Habermas’ concept of communicative action captures exactly this: understanding emerges where arguments are given time and space. In short-form formats, communication continues- often with enormous reach- but the channels through which it occurs have shifted.

“A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.” – Herbert A. Simon

Analysis increasingly degenerates into a tool for tabloid-style exaggeration. Headlines such as “THE NEW TACTIC,” “THE BEST PRESSING IN THE WORLD,” or “THIS IS MODERN FOOTBALL” suggest analysis but primarily follow market logic. Analyses are linguistically amplified as if they must be sold: the newest product, the best of its kind, faster, higher, further. Football as a consumer product is established – but now even the idyllic backyard of analysis? Marshall McLuhan’s famous dictum, “The medium is the message,” becomes particularly tangible here: the format determines not only the form, but increasingly also the content of analysis itself. The task is to reclaim analysis as a pursuit of understanding and curb its reduction to a consumable, attention-driven product – perhaps the challenge of the modern era is not to reinvent analysis, but to restore time, depth, and dialogical capacity to it.

To continue the metaphor of the idyllic backyard: analysis is increasingly turning into a bustling city. Here a street vendor, there a shop – no, I don’t want to buy anything. Help, where have I ended up? Everything crowded, everyone stressed, everyone caught in the rush of striving, of wanting. I just want the idyll: a coffee, some calm, a deep conversation. But the idyll is dead. Perhaps, as an analyst, one sometimes feels a certain emptiness – a metropolitan melancholy – the emptiness of overstimulated impersonality.

“The metropolitan is compelled by the economy of money exchange to a precision and objectivity that deprives personal life of its warmth.” – Georg Simmel, The Metropolises and the Intellectual Life, 1903

But let us zoom out again: I often experience this feeling on “X” or YouTube. There is an abundance of information, often highlighted for attention. Yet more information on complex topics does not automatically lead to more knowledge; it generates noise – a noise I described earlier in the metaphor. This constant noise simultaneously depletes the already scarce resource of attention and creates a perpetual stimulus environment, leading to a lack of contextualization and interpretation, while leaving many exhausted-another tactic video, another tweet, another reel on the best pressing? Phew – this “phew” is what science calls fragmented cognition. Algorithms naturally amplify extremes-even in sports: outrage, “ALL-CAPS HEADLINES,” or promotion drive engagement.

This critique is not aimed at users or analysts; we are all trapped in a system with incentive structures. Nevertheless, I want to draw attention to the growing bubbleization and ideological polarization of the analysis scene, amplified by extremes and a lack of contextualization. Quick accessibility and democratization lead to information, to knowledge, but this abundance also produces a depletion of theory and balance. We experience a pseudo – plurality in sport, an implied logic in the game that does not exist, manifested by algorithms – through likes and views.

A concrete example: relationism. A fascinating topic, scarcely explored-yet the mere word triggers algorithmic attention so heavily that it is used excessively, reducing it to a black-and-white concept and establishing a dogma, rather than allowing proper theoretical discussion. How do we get out of this situation? Everyone has taste, everyone has preferences – yes, everyone has their dogmas. We are human – accept it. As René Marić once said, dogmas can be dissolved by connecting them, by allowing different ideas to meet. Or as Jamie Hamilton puts it: perceive analysis as aesthetics. If we understand football as aesthetics, then football becomes art – but what is art? Art is the undefinable. And if we accept football as something without logic, we may at least free ourselves from established regimens of thinking and dogma. Don’t let yourselves be confined – feel the aesthetics.

“We live in a world where there is more and more information, and less and less meaning.” – Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation, 1981

If we turn to history, literary philosophy shows us that even the concept of freedom divides opinion – does freedom enable analysis, or does it simply reinforce the status quo and thereby prevent true analysis? Perhaps, however, this is not the real question. Maybe it is not about freedom versus non-freedom, but about whether we understand logic as the opposite of freedom. Logicimplies binary outcomes – true or false, right or wrong – and this stands in tension with the ‘spirit of play’. Play has rules and objectives, yet within the act of playing there are no universal truths. The growing sense of uniformity and rehearsal – the impression that everyone plays in similar ways – often creates the feeling that the game follows the rules of a single, universal logic, as if logic determines play rather than play shaping logic.

My concern is less about what is objectively right or wrong in football, and more about how we, as analysts and coaches, sometimes present our ideas as universal truths. By doing so, we implicitly suggest that there exists a pure logic within the game – a logic that may not fundamentally exist. I would argue that sport exists primarily to evoke emotions in those who play and those who watch – an experience that can be understood through aesthetics, where art becomes a counterpoint to logic, as Tolstoy suggested. This challenges the belief that results or success should stand above everything else and dictate our styles of play.

If there is no single ‘true’ way to play, then there can also be no single true analysis that fully dissects it into definitive parts. That is why we must give space to the diffuse edges – even at the risk of weakening clarity or precision in our explanations – and accept that not everything can be clearly identified or categorized, because pure logic does not exist here. Yet I firmly believe that by allowing more room for uncertainty and ambiguity within the game, we open ourselves to entirely new worlds of understanding. And precisely for this reason, it is all the more important to ask ourselves who we are-and what we want to be as analysts. We must no longer divide ourselves into “us” and “them,” but understand ourselves as a shared form of football observer. Hannah Arendt describes thinking as an activity that only unfolds in exchange, as something that emerges in the “in-between” of people. Analysis, therefore, is not a possession, but a process. We need to dare more again: recognize our own (natural!) weaknesses in reasoning, disclose our personal assumptions, and discuss more honestly with one another. Know more of what we do not know and never will.

For this reason, I am skeptical of sharply distinguishing between universally trained and didactically trained analysts – or of job advertisements favoring only one type. Pierre Bourdieu shows that fields tend to stabilize through differentiation rather than understanding; separation becomes a social marker rather than a question of quality. Class war! Is that really what we want? Pitting the professionalization of sport against an open culture? This runs all the way from coach education to analyst circles: those who were never professionals are excluded. Those who do not meet the standards in general education also do not meet the standards in football. It is a coupling of market logic with football – and we need a return to open football, even if this openness, in some places, requires a degree of self-criticism that is uncomfortable for some decision maker. Breaking out of established logics also means accepting that logic cannot be predetermined.

“Technology is never neutral; it always changes the conditions under which knowledge is recognized.” – Neil Postman, Technopoly, 1992

Attempts to standardize analysis this way lead to the imposition of linear thinking – a workflowization of analysis. The constant noise of information overload reinforces this effect. Increasingly, I observe a communicatively insulated bubble of club-based analysts, where external exchange is hardly desired. Yet the core of analysis is forgotten: “Thinking without communication is empty,” writes Jürgen Habermas-knowledge emerges in dialogue. Analysis thrives on joint dissection, on contradiction, and on critical (self-) questioning.

This text is not a judgment of the scene. Rather, it is an expression of unease-a self-reflective judgment. I, too, have long allowed myself to be guided by factions, by the pursuit of jobs, by the pursuit of attention, and I became dependent on it. Only when I became aware of this and adopted a more didactic path – without a goal beyond curiosity about the game – did new worlds of football open up to me. A curiosity expressed not in truths, but in provisional knowledge; in perspectives rather than dogmas; in theory as a tool rather than a label. Perhaps our strength should not lie in being faster, louder, or bigger. Perhaps it lies in withstanding the noise of the digital age. Where analysis no longer allows contradiction, it ends. But it also ends where analysis becomes mere consumption. But to end the text on a positive note – at the same time, there are more opportunities than ever before, more tactical cameras than ever, and more games to analyze than ever.

There have been discussions surrounding the importance of aesthetics as a branch of philosophy. Beauty is subjective and it has led to categorizations of protagonist and antagonist in the case of ball possession despite no concrete proof that control of the game belongs to teams with high possession. This has created villains and heroes; some have been/become victims of this categorization. Maybe in the place of aesthetics we can propose statistics. Considering that the scoreline is a statistic (with all the negative connotations around it e.g “lies, damned lies and statistics”- Mark Twain., it really has not stood a chance), analysis should be data/statistically driven as findings, conclusions and discussions will be more objective.

I did not add the context of the change in the world outside the football pitch, but I see Civilization goes down in 20-25 years. In Apocalypse No Data No Ai, the game resembles its origin.

#2629. Doc Rivers says 'difficult' Giannis Antetokounmpo 'didn't want to be the bad guy' while forcing Bucks exit

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Milwaukee Bucks coach Doc Rivers said Giannis Antetokounmpo was difficult to coach and "didn't want to be the bad guy" amid the saga that ultimately led to his trade to the Miami Heat this summer.

Rivers, who coached the Bucks for two and a half seasons from 2024-26, said on "The Bill Simmons Podcast" that the ordeal dragged on for so long because Antetokounmpo "kept yo-yoing" with his desire to leave Milwaukee. Antetokounmpo never publicly requested a trade.

Like any small-market star, Antetokounmpo had been the subject of trade rumors since he emerged as an MVP-caliber player, but the questions about his future really amped up in recent years as the Bucks' title window closed and he moved closer to unrestricted free agency.

The Bucks had the opportunity to trade Antetokounmpo after the 2024-25 season, which ended with another first-round exit after Damian Lillard tore his Achilles tendon. Instead, Milwaukee waived Lillard and stretched his contract, which will now be on their books until 2030, and signed Myles Turner to a four-year, $108 million deal in a desperate attempt to keep Antetokounmpo around. The plan did not work; the Bucks missed the playoffs last season for the first time since 2016, and eventually traded Antetokounmpo when it became clear that he would not sign an extension.

"In [Bucks general manager Jon Horst's] defense, I thought Giannis kept yo-yoing," Rivers said when discussing what went wrong in Milwaukee over the last few seasons. "When I look back on that whole situation, Giannis wanted out, but he was a Buck. He didn't want to be the bad guy. He wanted Jon and [co-owner Wes Edens] and those guys to say, 'We're trading you,' instead of him asking for a trade. To me, that was the game that was being played."

Everyone could see that Antetokounmpo, who led the Bucks to the 2021 NBA championship, was torn about leaving the only franchise he had ever known, and the city where he had spent nearly half of his life, but it's still notable to hear Rivers confirm it.

Rivers' more interesting comments were about how hard it was for him to coach Antetokounmpo:

"He's not easy. He plays at this crazy downhill pace. He's really a difficult guy. I was telling someone this. He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't necessarily have a super IQ at the same time. It's really a strange thing. And he really has only one way -- downhill, force, force, force. Every play, he wants to force it. I wish he'd learned how to execute better.

"He's one of those guys, you get a lot of them from the U.S., AAU guys that have never needed to execute, because they can do it on their own. But that doesn't help the team. I told Giannis this: The thing he still needs to learn is the value of execution. How important it is, when you're in practice and at shootaround, to lock in on execution. Now he has a coach who's as good as there is in execution."

Antetokounmpo is a unique player and, like many all-time greats, incredibly stubborn. Those qualities helped him grow into a two-time MVP and lead the Bucks to their first title in 50 years. They also made it challenging to build a roster around him and led him to play through injuries that should have kept him on the sideline.

There are certainly aspects of Antetokounmpo's style and approach that would make life difficult for any coach, but Rivers has been making excuses about his time with the Bucks since his introductory press conference, when he said, "I wouldn't wish this on anyone," about taking over a team with Antetokounmpo, Lillard and Khris Middleton mid-season.

It was also a bit strange to hear Rivers say that Antetokounmpo, who scored 50 points in a title-clinching game on 16 of 25 from the field and 17 of 19 from the free-throw line, needs to learn the value of execution.

Rivers was not retained after the 2026 season and Antetokounmpo, along with Bobby Portis, was traded to the Heat in June. In return, the Bucks received Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, three first-round picks, a second-round pick and a pick swap.

Both teams are off to rough starts this season. While the Bucks are 1-7 as they begin their rebuild, the Heat are 3-6. Antetokounmpo is averaging 27.3 points, 12.7 rebounds and 5.6 assists per game.

#2628. Antonio Brown avoids jail time, receives punishment after plea deal in Miami shooting

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former NFL wide receiver Antonio Brown will not serve jail time after he pleaded guilty Friday to a lesser charge stemming from a shooting incident at a boxing event in Miami last year.

The Super Bowl-winning ex-player was originally sought on one charge of attempted murder in May 2025 after a fight allegedly took place between Brown and several other individuals shortly after a celebrity boxing event. Brown pleaded guilty this week to aggravated assault with a firearm and received three years of probation.

Brown will undergo a mandatory psychological evaluation and may have to attend weekly counseling if mandated by a judge.

"My client was facing 30 years in prison with a 20-year minimum mandatory, and he was given an offer he just couldn't refuse," Brown's defense attorney, Mark Eiglarsh, told reporters. "Probation was too good to turn down, and we're both very excited about the outcome."

Videos from the altercation circulated on social media, as did pictures of Brown in handcuffs. Brown later posted on social media claiming he was jumped by people trying to take his jewelry.

"Regarding the boxing event that happened last night," Brown wrote at the time. "I was jumped by multiple individuals who tried to steal my jewelry and cause physical harm to me. Contrary to some video circulating, Police temporarily detained me until they received my side of the story and then released me. I WENT HOME THAT NIGHT AND WAS NOT ARRESTED.

"I will be talking to my legal council [sic] and attorneys on pressing charges on the individuals that jumped me. I will keep you all posted step-by-step on the process. Thank you for the support and love."

Brown last played in the NFL for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the 2021 season when he stormed off the field shirtless after getting into a heated argument with then-coach Bruce Arians.

He said he was returning to the league to play for the Baltimore Ravens in 2023, but nothing materialized. In June 2024, Brown filed for bankruptcy, blaming lawsuits and others for his financial misfortunes.

Five years prior to filing, Brown served an eight-game suspension for violating the league's personal conduct policy as a result of sexual and personal misconduct allegations levied against him.

From 2010-18 with the Pittsburgh Steelers, Brown was named to the Pro Bowl seven times and was a four-time All-Pro. He played for the New England Patriots for one game in 2019 before he was cut for sending threatening text messages to a woman. He spent his final two seasons with the Buccaneers.

#2627. MLB rumors: Tarik Skubal's market already hot, contenders eyeing Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a bit more than a week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

The market for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the offseason's best free agent, is already hot, according to the New York Post. Skubal is expected to sign in November, before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, though a deal is not imminent. Talks are underway, however, and his market is moving.

Skubal is expected to sign a record contract at least in total value, and possibly in average annual value. Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract ever given out. Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander's matching $43.3 million salaries with the Mets years ago set the record for the average annual value for a pitcher.

The Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, and Yankees are among the teams linked to Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports the New York Post. Unless MLB and the MLBPA unexpectedly avoid a lockout, Sato must sign before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Otherwise, he will return to the Hanshin Tigers for 2027.

We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available this offseason, and the best available position player. He has significant power but also swing-and-miss and defensive concerns at third base, similar to Munetaka Murakami a year ago. Murakami slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games as a rookie this season, providing proof of concept for Sato.

The Nationals have signed center fielder Jacob Young to a four-year extension, reports FanSided. The deal is worth $23 million and includes an $8 million club option for a fifth year. The extension buys out Young's three arbitration years and one free agent year, with a club option for a second free agent year. He's now under Washington's control through 2031.

Young, 27, has always been a superlative defender. He unlocked a new level on offense this season, particularly in the second half, when he hit .301 with a .385 on-base percentage. Young had been speculated as a trade candidate since last offseason, but the new extension locks him in as part of Washington's long-term core.

#2625. Is Drew Mestemaker really QB1? A troubling trend and lessons from Caleb Williams, Trevor Lawrence

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Caleb Williams. Trevor Lawrence. Drew Mestemaker.

Two former No. 1 overall picks and probably the hottest name in the 2027 NFL Draft all share a troubling distinction: Over the last decade-plus, only Williams and Lawrence had higher turnover-worthy-play rates under pressure in their final college seasons than Mestemaker has this year.

But there's a catch. For Williams and Lawrence, those numbers were one-year blips after considerably better performances earlier in their college careers. For Mestemaker, the mistakes have followed him from North Texas to Oklahoma State … and they've gotten worse.

None of that means Mestemaker can't be the first quarterback selected in the 2027 NFL Draft. He's put himself squarely in the QB1 conversation, and for good reason. I have Miami's Darian Mensah just ahead of him, but there's a whole lot to like about Mestemaker's game.

NFL teams will also have to answer an important question before investing a high first-round pick in him: What happens when defenses take away the easy throws and force him to make decisions under pressure?

There's plenty to like about the Oklahoma State quarterback, who spent last season at North Texas. For starters, Mestemaker looks the part. He has a strong arm, throws with anticipation and will get through his reads. He's comfortable attacking all three levels, manipulates defenders with his eyes and has the patience to stand in the pocket, reset his feet and deliver fastballs into tight windows.

Just watched Drew Mestemaker's throws vs. UCF, and he just keeps getting better. BTW, if Arch Manning had Mestemaker's tape, he'd be the consensus QB1, probably by a wide margin. Wrote about Mestemaker after he beat Oregon and he's playing better now. https://t.co/MPhvkXpD60

He has plenty of NFL-caliber throws on tape, especially on intermediate routes where he has to throw receivers open. It's easy to see why he's become a popular QB1 choice. But there are also stretches where he tries to do too much, and that's where the evaluation gets more complicated.

Through Week 9 of 2026, Mestemaker has seven turnover-worthy plays on 54 dropbacks when he was pressured, according to PFF. That's a 13.0% rate, more than double the 5.8% median for the first-round quarterbacks in our historical comparison.

(A turnover-worthy play isn't just an interception. It can be a dangerous throw that a defender drops or another mistake that puts the football at risk. And while the number itself doesn't tell us everything, it helps identify decisions that might otherwise get lost in the box score.)

Williams and Lawrence were the only first-rounders we looked at with higher rates in their final college seasons, but both had been considerably better the previous year. Williams went from 0.9% in 2022 to 15.3% in 2023, while Lawrence jumped from 1.6% in 2019 to 13.2% in 2020.

Turnover-worthy play percentage and yards per attempt when pressured

* 2026 season through Week 9. Source: PFF

Look at Williams and Lawrence now. Both had bumpy starts to their NFL careers, and both are now two of the NFL's best quarterbacks. It's a pretty good reminder that A.) landing in the right situation is probably the most important factor in a young QB's development, and B.) troubling college numbers don't mean you're destined to fail at the next level.

Mestemaker's struggles have followed him from North Texas to Oklahoma State. His turnover-worthy-play rate was 8.3% under pressure in 2025 before climbing to 13% so far this season. Over that span, he's put the ball in harm's way 13 times in 126 such situations. That's a 10.3% rate, and it's something NFL evaluators will have to consider.

Of course, there's recent precedent for NFL teams looking past troubling numbers. I wrote last November about Ty Simpson's historically poor deep-ball accuracy, and we later learned just how much injuries had affected his play. The Rams still took him 13th overall in April, betting on everything else he did well.

Here's what makes it even more interesting: Mestemaker has gotten much better at avoiding sacks, but he's also making more dangerous throws. Last season, he was sacked on roughly 21% of plays when pressured. That number is down to 11% this year, but while he's taking fewer sacks, he's also averaging a full yard less per pass attempt in those situations (5.6 to 4.5).

The tape provides more clues. Mestemaker generally shows good footwork and accuracy when he has time, and he's capable of working beyond his first read. But there are also moments when he forces throws into coverage instead of taking the easier completion underneath, or when his accuracy suffers because he doesn't get his feet set.

These aren't all necessarily mistakes caused by pressure, but they point to a similar concern: knowing when to challenge a defense and when to take what it's giving you.

The good news for Mestemaker is that other really talented quarterbacks have entered the NFL with concerns about their decision-making under pressure. A lot of them have gone on to be really good. Of course, not everyone develops the same way.

Let's start with Patrick Mahomes. In his final season at Texas Tech, he had an 8.5% turnover-worthy-play rate when pressured, but he also averaged 9.4 yards per attempt and generated 14 big-time throws. Mestemaker, by comparison, has averaged just 4.5 YPA this season, with three big-time throws against seven turnover-worthy plays.

Mahomes took risks, but he was also creating considerably more positive plays when things broke down. That's an important distinction because making dangerous throws is one thing; consistently making spectacular plays to offset those mistakes is another.

Jordan Love offers a different lesson. His final season at Utah State was a mess compared with his outstanding 2018 campaign. He went from 32 touchdowns and six interceptions to 20 touchdowns and 17 picks, and his turnover-worthy-play rate under pressure jumped from 3.4% to 10.9%.

Love averaged just 2.8 yards per attempt when pressured in 2019, even worse than Mestemaker this season. Green Bay still took him in the first round, betting on his physical talent and development. That patience paid off, a reminder that a concerning college season doesn't have to define a quarterback's NFL career.

Then there's Josh Allen, who happens to be Mestemaker's favorite quarterback. Allen inspired him to wear No. 17, and Mestemaker has talked about relating to Allen's unconventional football journey.

Allen's final college season wasn't nearly as productive as the one before. His passing yards fell from 3,203 to 1,812, his yards per attempt dropped from 8.6 to 6.7, and he completed just 56.3% of his passes. His turnover-worthy-play rate under pressure was 8.9%, yet Buffalo took him seventh overall because his physical tools were impossible to ignore.

Allen developed into JOSH ALLEN. While Mestemaker's best ball is likely in front of him too, it's unfair to expect anyone to make the leap Allen made once he arrived in the league.

Sam Darnold provides another example. His turnover-worthy-play rate under pressure was 10.5% in his final season at USC, but he also averaged 11.0 yards per attempt in those situations. Like Mahomes, he took chances, but he also made big plays when things broke down.

The point isn't that Mestemaker will become the next Mahomes, Allen, Love or Darnold. It's that quarterbacks can overcome weaknesses, but the risks have to be weighed against what they do well and what they're capable of becoming.

I still like Mestemaker a lot and there's every reason to believe he could be the first quarterback taken in either this draft or in 2028, should he decide to stay in school another year. But the mistakes under pressure are real, and they're going to be a part of his evaluation.

There's also time for him to get better, likely even a lot better. Remember, Mestemaker never started a varsity game at quarterback in high school; he was primarily a punter and safety before walking on at North Texas. He's already improved at avoiding sacks, and the next step is making smarter decisions when defenses disrupt his timing.

Mestemaker has the talent to be the first quarterback selected whenever he enters the draft. But making NFL throws and making NFL decisions aren't the same thing. And how much he improves his decision-making under pressure could ultimately determine just how early he'll hear his name called.

#2624. De schaduwzijde van relationisme (in de Nederlandse bekerfinale)

von Next Generation am 06.05.2026 in den Kategorien Eredivisie,SV Academy,Tactical Theory,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren

N.E.C. Nijmegen kon dit seizoen vanwege hun relationistische patronen en hun oplossingsstrategieën tegen mandekkingen met verticale positiewisselingen van hun centrale verdedigers op zich attent maken. Op de voorlaatste zondag ontmoetten zich in Rotterdam voor de Nederlandse bekerfinale AZ Alkmaar en het verrassende team van Nederland, N.E.C. Nijmegen. AZ won na een doelpunt uit een standaardsituatie in de eerste helft en goed uitgespeelde counters in de tweede helft uiteindelijk duidelijk met 5:1. Als kenner van de Nederlandse voetbalwereld heeft HH zich met de wedstrijd beziggehouden en beide teams nader onder de loep genomen.

N.E.C. speelde vanuit een 1-3-2-4-1 in balbezit en drukvol met man-tegen-man pressing, waarbij Linssen de keeper van AZ boogvormig aanliep. Over het algemeen probeerde N.E.C. bij elke gelegenheid door te drukken en in hun 1-1-structuur te komen. AZ had zich daarop ingesteld en hun 1-4-2-3-1-achtige basisformatie veranderd in een soort 1-4-2-2-2, waarbij Parrot en Daal de voorste linie vormden. AZ’s idee voor lange ballen tegen Nijmegens klassieke 1-1-pressing (intentie van balverovering in het directe duel door maximaal korte afstanden, onafhankelijk van dekking van de centrale, binnenste lijn) waren dwars- en diepteloopbewegingen tegen Nijmegens driemansdefensie (afgestemd op AZ’s 1-4-2-3-1), om maximaal veel verdedigers van Nijmegen te binden en vrije ruimtes naast en voor de laatste linie maximaal groot te maken. Daarbij driften Mijnans en Smit steeds weer slim in mogelijke kaats- of doorverbindingsruimtes voor en naast Parrot. Omdat Nijmegen vrijloopbewegingen direct volgde en geen collectieve laatste linie en hoogte koos, werden de verticale afstanden sterk uitgerekt. Vooral Sandler als centrale verdediger en directe tegenstander van Parrot fungeerde soms als libero ver achter zijn medeverdedigers. Een groot manco bij N.E.C. was sowieso dat een collectief opschuiven van de laatste linie, de organisatie van een gezamenlijke nieuwe hoogte niet of slechts zeer terughoudend en twijfelend plaatsvond. AZ maakte daar gebruik van met slimme loopwegen achter de lijnen en/of snel uitspelen van combinaties in de (grote) ruimte voor de laatste lijn van N.E.C.

De uitrekking en tegelijkertijd de fysieke aanwezigheid door Mijnans en Smit evenals de strijdlustige dubbele zes van Koopmeiners en Clasie kwam het 1-4-2-2-2 van AZ meer tegemoet. Soms leek het alsof juist deze verticale uitrekking (1-4-2-2-2, loopwegen van Parrot diep/wegtrekkend, Nijmegen zonder eigen buitenspellijn) evenals horizontale uitrekking (dwarslopen van Parrot, asynchroon/ aansluitend uitwijken van Mijnans) bewust door AZ gewild en voorbereid werd, doordat men vanuit een zeer brede 1-4-2-opbouw direct en vroeg lange passafstanden naar doelman Owusu-Oduro koos om het onmiddellijke aanlopen van Nijmegen (Linssen, waarbij de afstanden te groot waren om de bal serieus te kunnen onderscheppen) uit te lokken en daardoor eigen lange ballen goed te kunnen voorbereiden.

Wanneer AZ zich toch voor een korte opbouw besliste, vielen ze terug in een soort 1-3-1-opbouw met een naar binnen kwamende linkerback (de Wit). Opvallend was echter de duidelijke focus op de voorbereiding van lange ballen. Zo zocht bijvoorbeeld Koopmeiners in 1-3-2-opbouwmomenten, in plaats van de vrije ruimte te bezetten om druk te ontlasten, de directe weg naar voren om aanwezigheid voor tweede ballen te tonen.

AZ’s hybride 1-4-2-3-1 naar 1-5-2-2-1 als kryptoniet tegen N.E.C.

Bij balbezit van Nijmegen koos AZ voor een fundamentele spiegeling van N.E.C. Daarbij kozen zij voor een conservatief, mandekkend middenveldpressing. Terwijl Clasie (een zes van N.E.C.) en de beide tienen Daal en Mijnans (respectievelijk de halfverdedigers Dasa en Fonville) zeer klassiek vanuit het middenveldpressing balnabij mandekten en man-georiënteerd aanliepen, koos Parrot steeds weer slim voor diepere, passieve posities om alle wegen naar het centrum te sluiten.

Een bijzondere rol kwam toe aan Koopmeiners. Hij ging, uitgaande van een manoriëntatie tegen Nijmegens creatieve speler Chery, steeds weer bij de overgang naar een lager blok in de laatste linie en vormde zo een vijfmanslijn. In totaal ontstond zo een 1-5-2-2-1 in lagere fases van AZ door het terugvallen van Smit naar de dubbele zes met Clasie. Chery werd zo niet per se extreem mandekkend bewaakt, maar zijn actieradius naar voren werd beperkt en tegelijkertijd werd het noodzakelijke uitstappen van Koopmeiners uit de vijfmanslijn goed opgevangen.

De 1-5-2-2-1-structuur van AZ paste ook bij de meer relationistische intentie van N.E.C., waarbij het minder ging om balgeoriënteerde vrijloopbewegingen ten opzichte van elkaar, maar meer om vrij-radicaal een overtal in balnabijheid te creëren, minder afgestemd op elkaar of in relatie tot specifieke tegenstanderbewegingen/-posities. Zo kon de niet-balkant tien van AZ het centrum mede sluiten, loopwegen uit de opbouwlijn van N.E.C. onderscheppen en N.E.C.’s zessen dwingen om breder buiten het blok te spelen of hoger te positioneren, waardoor ze minder bij overtal situaties betrokken waren of de restverdediging verwaarloosden.

Tegelijkertijd was hij in de counter snel aanspeelbaar (korte maar verleggende passafstanden tegen counter-press na balwinst). De beide tienen van AZ waren verantwoordelijk voor het oppakken van de steeds weer verticaal opschuivende centrale verdedigers van N.E.C. In totaal slaagde AZ erin met deze structuur een +1 in de laatste linie te creëren, doordat Clasie zich dieper en eerder aan de niet-balkant tien (Lebreton) oriënteerde, Goes in de laatste lijn +1 tegen Linssen kon doorschuiven, de ruimte voor de verdediging met Smit werd verdicht en de beide centrale tienen het centrum sloten. Daarbij werd er minder geprobeerd om directe balveroveringen te realiseren, maar des te meer om acties naar voren te blokkeren en de balbezitter passief te controleren. Het leek alsof AZ langer probeerde de controle over posities en ruimtebezetting ten opzichte van elkaar te behouden dan N.E.C. dat met hun vele positiewisselingen en herstructureringen kon.

Wanneer AZ toch het pressingmoment activeerde, paste dat goed bij de opbouwstructuur van N.E.C. Meestal koos Parrot dan een centrum-sluitende, iets laargere positie ten opzichte van Sandler of een centrale verdediger van N.E.C. Wanneer N.E.C. vervolgens via de halfverdedigers indribbeld, werden de afstanden in hun eerste opbouwlinie automatisch groter. Het indribbelen van de halfverdedigers kon door de tienen van AZ goed worden opgevangen, een terugpass werd in de beweging door de eerder uitgestapte tien doorgelopen en Parrot nam verticale vervolgbewegingen van de passerende halfverdediger over. Door de grotere passafstand (door het vroege indribbelen) werd de loopactie van de passer minder effectief, omdat de bal langer onderweg was en de druk van AZ op (meestal) Sandler goed kon worden behouden. Korte passafstanden bij N.E.C. voor een lokkend spel en bewegen werden zo opgelost, mede omdat Nejasmic in pressingoplossingen als derde man geen sterke prestatie leverde. AZ liep echter vaak niet door tot Cillessen, die desondanks vaak zonder druk voor de lange bal koos (die zoals eerder beschreven geen effectief middel was).

Zonder indribbelen liep het voor N.E.C. ook niet beter, want doordat Sandler graag vanuit diepere posities lange passes probeert te spelen (Schlotterbeck-Vibes), moet N.E.C. bij het opschuiven grotere afstanden overbruggen met de laatste linie. Dit lukte slechts onregelmatig, waardoor de aansluiting van de laatste linie onvoldoende was.

Desalniettemin liet N.E.C. in de eerste helft, vaker via rechts, goede aanzetten zien om vanuit de zijkanten kansen te creëren. Een aanvallend probleem dat zich gedurende de hele wedstrijd voordeed, was dat acties vanaf de zijkant naar binnen niet ruimer (dus dynamisch ruimtes richting het centrum openen) of doelgerichter (loopacties in de rug van de balkant centrale verdediger) werden bevoordeeld. De aansluitende bewegingen om tegenstanders bewust weg te trekken van de vrijgespeelde zijkant kwamen te weinig voor. In plaats daarvan werden mogelijke passroutes naar binnen soms dichtgelopen door passief achter de bal aan te lopen (om een korte passoptie te zijn?). Een “Escadinha”, dus een diagonale positionering van meerdere spelers als een “ladder” naar voren, idealiter richting het doel, zou ook een goed middel zijn geweest om de relationistische patronen van N.E.C. om te zetten in gevaarlijkere situaties voor het doel, maar werd niet gecreëerd. Vooral via Sano als vrije, hoger doorschuivende, licht niet-balkant zes had men via een precieze halfspace-halfspace-verplaatsing (tegen mandekkingsteams sowieso altijd effectief) tot afwerkposities kunnen komen. Vooral links met Koopmeiners en rechts met Goes, die beiden bezig waren met het dekken op de lijn van de balkant nummer tien van N.E.C., had men goed ruimtes in hun rug kunnen bezetten en bespelen – zowel achter als voor de laatste linie van AZ. Een paar keer, wanneer het N.E.C. lukte om van buiten naar binnen achter de balkant centrale verdediger te opereren, werd het ook meteen gevaarlijk. Op die momenten werden door de duo’s van N.E.C. (N.E.C. gebruikt de duo’s op de zijkant enigszins vergelijkbaar met Bayern in voor- of achterlopende, doorlopende bewegingen) (Ouaissa-Chery/Dasa en Önal-Lebreton/Fonville) natuurlijke verdedigingsmechanismen uitgelokt (achter de back spelen = centrale verdediger die uitstapte zal waarschijnlijk in de laatste lijn terugvallen, afdekken of doordekken), waardoor N.E.C., gecombineerd met goed wegbewegen van de tegenstander, zich in de rug van de verdediging enkele (halve) kansen kon creëren. AZ loste deze kleine problemen in de controle op doordat Clasie zich als niet-balkant zes toch meer balgeoriënteerd positioneerde, en Lebreton minder klassiek volgde.

Lange ballen van N.E.C. tegen een al terugzakkend AZ, dat snel naar achteren liep om diepte te sluiten, waren niet kansrijk – noch dynamisch noch numeriek.

In de tweede helft probeerde N.E.C. meer via een opdribbel van Fonville over de linkerkant te overloaden. Nejasmic koos een duidelijk meer centrumhoudende positionering in balbezit (zessen gestaffeld), Lebreton speelde als linker wing-back, de ingevallen Willumsson iets dieper, vermoedelijk om Goes van AZ uit de verdediging te trekken. Sano, de oprukkende Fonville en gedeeltelijk ook Chery namen deel aan de overload links. Een intentie leek te zijn om links aan te lokken om vervolgens rechts uit te spelen en Ouaissa in 1-tegen-1-duels te krijgen. Koopmeiners volgde Chery echter niet consequent, N.E.C. stond gedeeltelijk met 6-7 spelers in de linker halfspace, omdat zelfs Dasa (!) naar die kant ging. De bewegingen in deze overload waren echter zelden goed genoeg op elkaar afgestemd. De nog steeds aanwezige ruimtes (ook omdat AZ al vroeg balnabij met hun 4/5-mansketen kantelde en beide backs de Wit en Dijkstra individuele zwaktes hebben in het verdedigen van de rug) van buiten naar binnen in de rug (achter of voor de verdedigingslinie van AZ) van de half-uitstappende Goes werden te zelden consequent bespeeld of pas te laat bezet. Voorwaartse, boogvormige bewegingssequenties rondom een doelspeler, die positiegetrouw een ruimte bezet en als kaatsspeler fungeert, werden niet ingezet, waardoor alle bewegingen ten opzichte van elkaar geïmproviseerd of fragmentarisch leken. Wanneer men er eenmaal in slaagde een pocket in de halfspace tussen meerdere AZ-spelers te openen, werd deze geopende ruimte niet verder benut door bijvoorbeeld een tegenstanderbindende loopactie achter deze ruimte, maar probeerde elke speler eerder een beetje dominant de bal op te halen en verder te passen. Kort gezegd waren er veel dominante spelers die allemaal graag de bal direct en zonder intentie van elkaar wilden hebben. Aanvullende, ondersteunende intenties bij spelers waren zeldzaam. Waar men in de eerste helft nog vroeg een flankbezetting koos en zo een duo op de flank ruimte gaf, was Linssen nu de enige speler van N.E.C. in de box tegen AZ, dat consequent een +1 behield. Wanneer N.E.C. via de goed, maar nog te terughoudend, niet tot het einde van het mogelijke oprukpotentieel indribbelende Fonville wist op te rukken, ontbrak het aan activiteit en aansluitende bewegingen om via een snelle korte verplaatsing van afzakkende/verbindende zessen/centrale verdedigers de ontstane ruimtes in het centrum te bespelen. Vooral Willumsson bood hier geen goede passopties, hoewel hij zich in kansrijke ruimtes bevond. Ondanks het gebrek aan doorbraak kon N.E.C. meer controle over de wedstrijd verkrijgen en AZ enigszins naar achteren drukken. AZ daarentegen ging vanaf ongeveer de 55e minuut als reactie agressiever pressen, Goes volgde in hogere middenveldpressingfasen Willumsson ver naar voren. N.E.C. slaagde er niet in om tijdig in mandekking-oplossende patronen te komen, ook het spel via de extra speler Cillessen bracht geen verlichting. De communicatie van Sano en Nejasmic met betrekking tot afgestemd vrijlopen en vrijmaken, bewegingen naar de bal, liet te wensen over.

De invalbeurt van Willumsson bracht echter defensieve meerwaarde. De 193 cm grote IJslander kon bij lange ballen van AZ meer ruimte afdekken en met grotere actieradius meer aanwezigheid tonen bij tweede ballen, zonder gaten in de mandekking als tien op AZ’s zessen te trekken. N.E.C. paste namelijk Nejasmic aan in de rol van ondersteunende speler van Sandler. De zes koos nu zijn positioneringen zodanig dat hij direct rond/met Sandler tegen Parrot verdedigde en hem afschermde, waardoor vaak een soort viermanslijn bij N.E.C. ontstond, wat AZ voorlopig in toom hield.

N.E.C. probeerde nog steeds van links naar rechts uit te spelen. Helaas moesten ze de problemen in de restverdediging evenals de lasten van hun over-overload duur bekopen, omdat AZ twee keer na een verplaatsing naar Ouaissa balveroveringen boekte, counters startte en N.E.C.’s individuele rest-mandekking uiteindelijk meedogenloos afstrafte met de doelpunten voor 2:0 en 3:0. Vooral bij het tweede doelpunt werd duidelijk dat de individuele oriëntatie op de tegenstander, bijna onafhankelijk van de balpositie op het veld en zonder collectieve afstemming, duidelijke nadelen met zich meebrengt. Sowieso is mandekking rond het eigen zestien een minder logisch middel – zonder baldruk en collectieve hoogtebepaling van een laatste verdedigingslinie wordt het een uitnodiging om kansen te creëren. Bij de 2:0 door Mijnans lag het centrum voor het doel van Nijmegen open, bij de 3:0 werd er niet onderling gekanteld. Aan beide doelpunten ging echter een overloadpoging links vooraf, beter gezegd een over-overloadpoging. Klassieke overloadings met één, misschien twee extra spelers hebben als effect de tegenstander (idealiter) kort in een buitenruimte te binden zonder dat hij toegang tot balverovering heeft, vervolgens in voorbereide structuren (passafstanden zo groot als mogelijk voor zo min mogelijk balstops, maar zo kort als nodig om het overloadingseffect te benutten) te verplaatsen en de vrijere kant via 1-tegen-1, kleine-aantallenpatronen of voorzetten uit de halfspace te benutten. Bij een over-overload in de zin van het relationisme gaat het minder om goed gebalanceerde verplaatsingsstructuren, kleine-aantallenpatronen op de vrijere kant of een gezonde numerieke verhouding, maar om het doorspelen aan de overload kant. N.E.C. over-overload links, verplaatste dan relatief ruim (dus niet kort) via de centrale verdedigers via Dasa naar Ouaissa, waarbij AZ kortstondig een numeriek overwicht had aan de “vrijere” rechterkant. Bij balbezit van Ouaissa vóór de 2:0 stonden 5 (!) spelers van N.E.C. nog links functieloos, niet betrokken naast elkaar – dus ook aansluitende bewegingen om kleine-aantallenpatronen te ondersteunen of doelgerichte loopacties en voorzetvoorbereidingen ontbraken. Sandler, die de verplaatsing bij de 2:0 inleidde, liep na zijn pass naar de zijkant door naar voren (kennelijk een principe van Nijmegen). Echter op zo’n manier dat hij Ouaissa in het 1-tegen-1 blokkeerde, daarna niet als ondersteunende speler fungeerde en eigenlijk enigszins doelloos voor hem stond. Door de loopactie van Sandler liet Nejasmic zich duidelijk in de laatste linie zakken en ook Dasa zag ervan af om Ouaissa korter te ondersteunen, waardoor hij in een 1-tegen-2 terechtkwam. Uiteindelijk leidde dit door de ondertal-situatie tot balverlies van Nijmegen – mede door het ontbreken van een “bodyguard” van Dasa. Sandler stond voor de bal, het centrum was onbezet, AZ kon eenvoudig naar voren spelen en aanvallen – doordat het in de restverdediging ontbrak aan situatie-inzicht (Nejasmic) en consequente afdekking. Uiteindelijk verslechterde Sandlers loopactie de situatie eerder.

Ook aan de derde tegentreffer ging een verplaatsing van links naar rechts vooraf, dit keer liep Dasa als passer niet door – wat in tegenstelling tot Sandler bij de tweede tegentreffer passend zou zijn geweest – maar bood zich opnieuw kort aan – echter verloor Ouaissa zich opnieuw in een ondertal-dribbel (individuele besluitvorming, maar ook weinig ondersteuning). Dit keer was de situatie echter ideaal voor counter-press, waartoe de omliggende Nijmegen-spelers ook besloten, alleen dekte Dasa niet door, waardoor AZ min of meer gecontroleerd kon uitspelen. Met enig geluk wist AZ, opnieuw achter de laatste verdediger (Sandler) van N.E.C., maar nog op eigen helft, door te spelen en de 3:0 te maken. In het vervolg probeerde Nijmegen alles, maar behalve korte hoop na de 3:1 kwam er niets meer.

N.E.C. draaide zo ver aan de knop van positiewisselingen dat het bijna oververhit raakte. Constante over-overloads, nieuwe posities, verticaal doordribbelende centrale verdedigers uit een driemansopbouw zijn een grote, in deze wedstrijd tegen een slim verdedigend AZ, te grote last om tegelijkertijd spelritme, veldcontrole en restorganisatie in het oog te houden. Te veel spelers, bijvoorbeeld Sano als linker, afzakkende zes uit de overload, die bij balbezit van Ouaissa twee keer niet consequent genoeg naast de laatste verdediger van N.E.C. doorschoof voor een 2-tegen-1-afdekking, moeten in situaties verdedigen of aanvallen (Sandler voor de 2:0) die te vreemd/te ongeschikt of te veeleisend zijn qua situatiedynamiek voor hun profiel.

Desondanks is Nijmegen een team dat zich door hun vrij-radicale speelstijl heeft toegelegd op aantrekkelijk, onderhoudend voetbal. Uitstekende aanzetten zouden offensief door eenvoud, consistentie (positiegetrouwheid) en teamorganisatie (ritme van de aanvalsrichting, balans van overloads) kunnen worden verbeterd. Defensief zou een collectiviteit van de laatste linie zijn intrede moeten doen. Mocht dit in de toekomst lukken, zal N.E.C. niet alleen als een van de spannendste teams van Nederland voor ophef zorgen, maar ook in Europa. Als derde in de Eredivisie zijn ze in ieder geval op de goede weg.

HH groeide op aan de Nederlandse grens, maar oriënteerde zich tactisch liever richting Zuid-Europa. Naast freelancewerkzaamheden voor Duitse profclubs is hij sinds twee jaar ook actief als jeugdtrainer bij de O17 van N.E.C. Nijmegen

#2623. Knicks defend Taylor Swift after Tyler Kolek, Deuce McBride characterize her fandom as 'performative'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Knicks have released a statement supporting Taylor Swift's fandom after recent comments from reserve guards Tyler Kolek and Deuce McBride.

"Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organization," a Knicks spokesperson said.

Earlier this month, Kolek called Swift's fandom "a little performative" on an NBA 2K League video. Kolek and McBride were playing a game called "Deflected," where they have to compete in NBA 2K to avoid answering awkward questions. After McBride scored on the game, Kolek had to answer: "Who's the fakest celebrity fan you've seen sitting courtside in an NBA game?"

"At the Knicks games, I would say it's very performative," Kolek said. "Because they just want to be seen at the game; they're not necessarily fans. Maybe Taylor Swift?"

"I don't know if I've seen her at any other games," Kolek said.

"Swifties not gonna like that answer," McBride replied.

"No, I'm gonna get some hate from the Swifties," Kolek acknowledged. "I get she's got a lot going on, so she can't come all the time, but it's a little performative."

This is not the first time Swift's Knicks fandom has been questioned. "She's not a Knicks fan. Get outta here, girl," broadcaster Monica McNutt said in June after Swift sat courtside during Game 4 of the 2026 NBA Finals, which the Knicks won with a historic 29-point comeback. McNutt later apologized for the comments.

Swift was born and raised in Pennsylvania, but has been a Knicks fan since moving to New York over a decade ago. Here's an excerpt from an interview with Time Magazine in 2014:

You recently moved to New York. Are you a Knicks fan now?

I love them, though. Why does that matter? So you run into a bunch of different, interesting types of people at the Met Ball. I've gone the last four years. And the most normal people at that event, every single time, are Amar'e Stoudemire and his wife Alexis. I talk with them and hang with them every time I'm there. So I've always had this sort of love of the Knicks, just because Amar'e is so cool. And also I performed at the Knicks'—at Madison Square Garden's—Kids Talent Competition at halftime when I was 12 or 13. And ever since then I've had this kind of sparkly, magical opinion of Madison Square Garden and the Knicks, since they let me sing when I was a little kid.

Swift and Kansas City Chiefs star Travis Kelce were married at Madison Square Garden during a lavish wedding in July.

#2622. Warriors' Kristaps Porziņģis stepping away from basketball to deal with ongoing health issues

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Golden State Warriors big man Kristaps Porzingis announced Friday that he has "made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love" as he continues to deal with mysterious health issues. It's unclear when, or if, the 31-year-old Porziņģis will return to the court.

Porziņģis has not played for the Warriors this season and reports earlier this week indicated that the team is withholding payments from him. He signed a two-year, $40 million deal with the Warriors in free agency this summer, but the second year of the deal only has a $3 million guarantee.

Here is Porziņģis' full statement announcing his decision to step away from basketball:

This season I was really looking forward to running it with this group, but as I ramped up, my body didn't respond the way I anticipated.

I'm doing good, but I know what it takes, and I'm not where I want to be to perform at the level that I expect from myself. At this point, I've made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love.

In this situation, I want to show the utmost respect for the Golden State Warriors and work with them to find a solution that makes sense.

I'm thankful to my family and close ones for always being there. Much appreciation to all of you for the support.

Porziņģis' career has been defined by health problems. He's played more than 57 games just three times since he was drafted No. 4 overall by the New York Knicks in 2015, and has dealt with significant injuries, including a torn ACL that cost him the entire 2018-19 season. In recent years, he's been limited by this mysterious illness that first became an issue in Boston during the 2024-25 season.

Porziņģis started dealing with extreme fatigue and previously disclosed a diagnosis of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS, which is characterized by rapid changes in heart rate when a person stands up and can lead to exhaustion and dizziness.

"You know how people say, 'Oh, I'm so fatigued.' I've never used those words. I don't even like to speak in those terms, but I really was like that," Porziņģis said ahead of last season. "At that time, I could just lay on the couch and be a house cat."

Over the last three seasons with the Celtics, Atlanta Hawks and Warriors, Porziņģis has only played 74 games. He has been away from the Warriors since late September and released a previous statement in mid-October shutting down rumors that he had been diagnosed with HIV or AIDS. At that point, the Warriors said Porziņģis would be out indefinitely.

"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap. Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon," Porziņģis wrote. "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support."

The Warriors hoped that Porziņģis would play a big role this season as a floor-spacing big, especially while Jimmy Butler (torn ACL) and Moses Moody (torn patellar tendon) remain sidelined. Instead, it seems more likely that he will never play for the franchise again.

The Warriors have reportedly been trying to trade Porziņģis to use his $20 million cap figure, as explained by CBS Sports' Sam Quinn:

While he would not have trade value as a player given his health status, he is essentially an expiring contract with only that small $3 million guarantee on the books for next season. That could potentially make him valuable to a team looking to move off of longer-term money, or the Warriors could entice another team into a trade using draft picks with Porziņģis serving only as the matching salary.

Despite Porziņģis' absence, the Warriors are off to a 6-3 start, putting them in seventh place in the extremely crowded Western Conference standings. Rookie big man Yaxel Lendeborg has stepped up in Porziņģis' place and provided a major boost on both ends of the floor.

Through nine games, Lendeborg is averaging 21 points, 7.1 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 1.1 steals while shooting 49.2% from the field, including 39.6% from 3-point range.
